6.0 PROCESSING FILES 
6.1 Transferring files from DACU to the MLC 
All files will be automatically transferred from th e DACU to C:\ftp on the MSG laptop. Housekeeping 
files (.hkp) are transferred on the hour and upon shut down (with either the shutdown or restart option). 
The Log file is also transferred upon shutdown. P- Trak, DustTrak, and heater files are transferred soon 
after they are created. P-Trak and DustTrak file s are not automatically created since their data is 
embedded in the housekeeping data. To explicitly retrie ve logged data select the Transfer Data button on 
the DustTrak and P-Trak tabs. This should be do ne no more frequently than once per minute because the 
filename is derived from the GMT, including the latest minute, but not the latest second. 
If you need the data immediately or a file doesn’t get downlinked for some reason you’ll have to do it 
manually using one of two methods described here: 
6.1.1 Using SAMEDisplay and FTP Cmd command. 
You’ll need to identify what file you need and the dir ectory it is in. Files are stored in a

passages.title: SAME Operations Manual 007
passages.text:
ing one of two methods described here: 
6.1.1 Using SAMEDisplay and FTP Cmd command. 
You’ll need to identify what file you need and the dir ectory it is in. Files are stored in a directory named 
according to GMT year and day. For instance /data/2006_132/. The .log file will be named 
2006_132_00.log in this example. Housekeeping files will be 2006_132_15.hkp, 2006_132_16.hkp, etc. 
according to the GMT. 
With the flight software and SAMEDisplay running (does not need to be Initialized), select the FTP Cmd 
from the System tab. Type: LCD /data/2006_132, for example, to change local directory (on the DACU) 
and send the command. Then select FTP Cmd again a nd type: PUT 2006_132_16.hkp, for example, and 
send the command. Watch your letter case – it matters. 
6.1.2 Using SAME processor command line to transfer files 
For this to work you’ll need a keyboard and mon itor connected to the GSE port on the SAME DACU. 
Also, verify that the switch on the SAME DACU is sw itched to Override position. This is obviously a 
ground use only method. 
From the command line on the GSE monitor (if th

passages.title: SAME Operations Manual 007
passages.text:
ACU. 
Also, verify that the switch on the SAME DACU is sw itched to Override position. This is obviously a 
ground use only method. 
From the command line on the GSE monitor (if the so ftware is running you can get another console 
window by typing <CTRL><ALT>n, where n is 1 or 2), navigate using cd and ls to the directory with the 
file you want to transfer. Type: ftp 192.168.1.1 <Enter>. Type: anonymous<Enter> for name and just 
<Enter> for password. Then at ftp> prompt t ype: bin<Enter>, then t ype: put 2006_ 132_16.hkp, for 
example. File should end up in C:\SAME Data on laptop. After done transferring file(s), type:

7.3.3 Secondary Aging Volume 
When a secondary aging period and volume are speci fied, the piston must stop a percentage of the 
distance between the top and bottom of the chamber. There is no direct physical measurement of the 
running distance, therefore it is estimated from th e exhaust rate over time. The registry value, 
ExhaustPercentageCorrectionFactor, is applied to the running percentage. To adjust this value, 
- Perform a SelfTest to exhaust the chamber to a specific percentage. For best results use the 
exhaust rate and secondary volume that will be used during the actual test. Or use 5 LPM and 
50%. 
- Perform a SelfTest to exhaust the chamber the rest of the way. Use the same rate and 100%. 
- Calculate the time taken for each portion using log messages or pressure data and figure the 
percentage of total time taken by the second exhaust. Adjust the registry value and repeat until 
this percentage is within the desired accuracy of the secondary aging volume percentage.

Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) 
 
 
Abstract 
 
Leaks, fires, and spills are some of the most significant hazards that must be accounted for in the 
design of the environmental control and life-su pport system on spacecraft. While prevention is 
certainly the first line of defens e against a fire, early detection of a overheat event or an actual 
fire allows the crew to res pond before the hazard gets out of control. The limited options 
available for response to a spacecraft fire increas e the importance of dete cting the fire in an 
earlier stage of its development than is typical for terrestrial applications. This report describes 
the outcomes of the Smoke Aerosol Measurements Experiment (SAME), an experiment 
conducted in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) on the International Space Station (ISS) 
to characterize the size distribution of smoke part iculate produced in low- gravity from a variety 
of overheated spacecraft material s The absence of gravity can im pact not only the formation of 
the smoke particulate but also th e aging and coagulation proc

passages.title: SAME Final Science Report
passages.text:
ity from a variety 
of overheated spacecraft material s The absence of gravity can im pact not only the formation of 
the smoke particulate but also th e aging and coagulation processes that occur as the particulate 
are transported from their source to a detector. 
 
Based on the results of an earlier flight project carried out in th e Glovebox of the Space Shuttle, 
(Comparative Soot Diagnostics (CSD)), the soot particles gene rated and observed in low gravity 
environment tend to be larger in size than t hose in earth conditions. Ho wever, the preliminary 
results of CSD project were not conclusive because of a minor variation of the temperature of hot 
wire which heated the test sample to generate smoke, and also because the CSD apparatus could 
not measure the liquid drops existing in the smoke produced by several of the samples. 
Furthermore, the CSD project was not designed to provide on-orbit measurement of the particle 
size distribution. The Smoke Aerosol Measurement E xperiment was designed to obtain this data 
that could then be used to design the next-generation smoke de

passages.title: SAME Final Science Report
passages.text:
ement of the particle 
size distribution. The Smoke Aerosol Measurement E xperiment was designed to obtain this data 
that could then be used to design the next-generation smoke detectors for space exploration 
missions. Unfortunately, because of the relati vely small volume of the MSG, it cannot 
accommodate the instruments normally used in a ground-based laboratory to measure the size 
distribution of smoke particul ate. Therefore, a new proce dure was developed, the moment 
method, from which the characteristics of the part icle size distribution can be inferred using a 
minimum number of portable instrument. 
 
The SAME experiments were conducted during E xpedition 15 on the ISS. Four materials, 
typical of those found in spacecr aft, were tested including cellulose (lamp wick), Kapton, 
silicone rubber, and Teflon. A fift h material, dibutyl-phthalate (D BP) retained in a cotton wick 
was used as a reference. In order to simulate the detection of a pre-fire overheated-material event, 
samples were heated to temperatures below th e ignition point. The smoke generation conditions

passages.title: SAME Final Science Report
passages.text:
erence. In order to simulate the detection of a pre-fire overheated-material event, 
samples were heated to temperatures below th e ignition point. The smoke generation conditions 
were controlled to provide repeatable sample surface temperatures and air flow conditions. The 
transport time from the smoke source to the det ector was simulated by holding the smoke in an 
aging chamber for times ranging from 10 seconds to 1800 seconds. Smoke particle samples 
were collected on Transmission Electron Microsc ope (TEM) grids for post-flight analysis. The 
smoke properties were measured using particulat e aerosol diagnostics that measure different 
moments of the size distribution. These statistic s were combined to determine the geometric 
mean particle sizes and geometric standard devia tion, which is sufficient to describe the entire 
smoke distribution if a lognormal distribution is assumed. For comparison, smoke detectors from

passages.title: SAME Final Science Report
passages.text:
iv 
 
the ISS and the space shuttle we re also included in the SAME apparatus. The experimental 
results show that, for the materials tested, a su bstantial portion of the smoke particles are below 
500 nm in diameter. The smoke transport model demonstrated that mixing dominates the smoke 
transport and that consequently detection time lags are longer than in normal gravity. The 
knowledge gained from SAME can be used to es tablish design requirements for smoke detectors 
used in future spacecraft.

1. Introduction 
 
Appropriate design of fire detection systems require s knowledge of both the expected signature of the 
events to be detected and the bac kground levels of the measured parame ters. Terrestrial fire detection 
systems have been developed based on extensive study of terrestrial fires. 1, 2 Unfortunately, there is no 
corresponding data set for spacecraft fires and cons equently current spacecraft fire detectors were 
developed based upon experience on normal gravity fi re behavior and propertie s. This approach was 
necessary given the absence of data concerning microgravity smoke particulate. However planned 
spacecraft and their planned missions outside of low earth-orbit will requi re increased reliability of fire 
detection systems in addition to robust false alar m resistance. Extended lunar-surface missions will 
require systems that are not influenced by lunar dust and other nuisance dust sources. 
The absence of buoyant flow increas es the residence time in microgra vity fires causing substantial 
changes in flame structure. Given the large changes in fir

passages.title: SAME Final Science Report
passages.text:
ance dust sources. 
The absence of buoyant flow increas es the residence time in microgra vity fires causing substantial 
changes in flame structure. Given the large changes in fire beha vior seen in reduced gravity, it is 
reasonable to expect that the signatures and detection requirements of these fires will change. There are 
a number of factors that can be expected to aff ect the particle size distri bution of the smoke from 
spacecraft fires. The absence of buoyant flow in low-gravity increases the residence time in 
microgravity fires and increases the transit ti me from the reaction zone to the detector. 3 The materials 
used in spacecraft are different from those typically used in terrestrial applications where smoke 
properties were previously evaluate d. More importantly, the limited options available to respond to a 
spacecraft fire increase the importance of detecting the fire in an earlier stage of its development than is 
typical for terrestrial applications. All of these effects can be expected to change the smoke particle size 
distribution. The objective of this work

passages.title: SAME Final Science Report
passages.text:
e of its development than is 
typical for terrestrial applications. All of these effects can be expected to change the smoke particle size 
distribution. The objective of this work was to ma ke sufficient measurements of smoke from spacecraft 
fires to enable improved design of future detectors. 
2. Smoke Background 
 
Smoke is a general term that encompasses aerosol materials produced by a number of processes. In 
particular for non-flaming combustion, the aerosol incl udes recondensed original material or pyrolysis 
products that can be either liquid or solid. For flaming combustion, the aerosol includes soot particulate, 
condensed water vapor, and ash particles. Soot part icles dominate the smoke pa rticulate in established 
flaming fires while unburned pyrolysis products and recondensed polymer frag ments are produced by 
smoldering and pyrolysis in the early stage of fi re growth. Given the constrained space on any 
spacecraft, the target for the fire detection system is necessarily the early phase and not established 
flaming fires; consequently, the primary target for detecti

passages.title: SAME Final Science Report
passages.text:
d space on any 
spacecraft, the target for the fire detection system is necessarily the early phase and not established 
flaming fires; consequently, the primary target for detection is the pyrolysis products and not the soot. 
 
The background regarding fire detection in US spacecraft is summarized in this paper but is discussed in 
more detail in papers by Friedman and Urban 4, 5 In the Mercury, Gemini a nd Apollo missions, the crew 
quarters were limited and mission durat ions were short, consequently it was considered reasonable that 
the astronauts would rapidly detect any fire. The S kylab module, however, included approximately 30 
UV-sensing fire detectors. 4 These devices were limited to line-of -sight and were reported to have 
difficulties with false alarms. 
 
Details of the ISS and STS detector require ments are described by Steisslinger et al. 6 A brief overview 
of the requirements is given below.

passages.title: SAME Final Science Report
passages.text:
2 
 
Space Shuttle Detectors: 
At the time the Space Shuttle Orbiter (Space Tran sportation System (STS)) was developed, smoke 
detection for terrestrial applic ations was becoming commonplace. 1 In particular, ionization detectors 
were readily available but photoelectric 
(scattering or obscuration detectors) were 
generally unavailable due to the difficulty of 
producing stable light sources. There were 
no data available concerning the smoke or 
dust particle size dist ribution in low-gravity 
and the database for normal-gravity smoke 
characteristics was a fraction of what is 
available today. Consequently, the STS 
smoke detector (Fig. 1) employed a variant 
of the accepted ground-based approach 
(ionization detectors). The Orbiter has nine 
particle-ionization smoke detectors in 
avionics cooling air return lines in the mid-
deck and flight deck and the SpaceLab had 
six additional partic le-ionization smoke 
detectors in the avionics lines. 7 While the 
design rationale is not completely known, 
Celesco™ (later Brunswick Defense™) 
based their design on data that suggested 
i

passages.title: SAME Final Science Report
passages.text:
on smoke 
detectors in the avionics lines. 7 While the 
design rationale is not completely known, 
Celesco™ (later Brunswick Defense™) 
based their design on data that suggested 
incipient fires could be discriminated by looking for particulate in the 0.4 μm to 0.7 μm range.8 The use 
of a pump provided the opportunity to use a particle separator that re jected particulate larger than 1 μm. 
This air pump increased the power requirements a nd reduced the operational lif e of the detector. The 
STS detector as built was designed to alarm at a particle loading of 2 mg/m 3 for 5 seconds (based on 1 
micron particles) or a 0.022 mg/m3/s rise in concentration for 20 seconds9. 
 
ISS Detectors: 
The International Space Station (ISS) smoke detector de sign took advantage of the availability of stable 
laser-diode light sources, mirroring a tr end in terrestrial detectors toward light scattering devices. This 
provided the opportunity to produce a detector that required substantially less power, (1.5 Watts versus 9 
Watts for the orbiter detector) 6 and, with no moving parts, was quiet er wi

passages.title: SAME Final Science Report
passages.text:
ided the opportunity to produce a detector that required substantially less power, (1.5 Watts versus 9 
Watts for the orbiter detector) 6 and, with no moving parts, was quiet er with a much longer operational 
life. The choice was supported by data indicating that early smoldering fires produce larger particulate 
than established flaming fires. 1 The ISS detectors (Fig. 2) are lase r-diode, forward-scattering, smoke or 
particulate detectors. The sensitivity extends down to 0.3 μm but is greatest for particles larger than 1 
μm. The current requirements for the ISS call for tw o detectors in the open ar ea of the module, and 
detectors in racks that have cooling air-flow.10 
 
The design developed for the ISS by Allied Signal™ (Fi g. 2) consists of a 2-pass laser diode to sense 
forward scattered light ( 30 degrees). There is also a light tran smission sensor to monitor the beam 
intensity. The system is designed to alarm base d on the magnitude of th e scattered light signal 
referenced to the beam intensity. The system is less se nsitive to particles smaller than the wavelength of

passages.title: SAME Final Science Report
passages.text:
esigned to alarm base d on the magnitude of th e scattered light signal 
referenced to the beam intensity. The system is less se nsitive to particles smaller than the wavelength of 
the laser (near IR) than it is to larger particles. The mini mum reported sensitivity is 0.3 μm.6 The ISS 
detector was designed to alarm at 1% obscuration per foot using an Underwriters Laboratory (UL)

NASA orbiter fleet. The inlet is on the right and the gas is

smoke box and white light extinction. This 
was implemented using a transfer standard 
detector and a 0.5 m polystyrene-bead 
aerosol system that was used to set the 
amplifiers on each unit. The transfer 
standard was calibrated in the smoke box 
and then used to set the levels with the 
aerosol system. 
 
As a result of these de sign decisions, the ISS 
and the Orbiter detectors have particle 
sensitivities that do not overlap. In both 
cases the designs were based upon the best 
available data at the time. However, due to 
the complete absence of low-g data 
concerning the nature of particulate and 
radiant emission from incipient and fully 
developed low-g fires, different conclusions 
were drawn concerning the optimal design 
for spacecraft fire detection. 
 
As described by Friedman 4 there have been 
six overheat and failed component failures in 
the NASA Orbiter fleet in addition to several 
similar incidents that have occurred on the 
ISS. None of these events spread into a real fire but as mission durations in crease, the likelihood of 
failures increases. The experie

imilar incidents that have occurred on the 
ISS. None of these events spread into a real fire but as mission durations in crease, the likelihood of 
failures increases. The experience on Mir in 1997 has shown that fa ilure of oxygen generation systems 
can have significant consequences. As a result, impr oved understanding of spac ecraft fire detection is 
critically needed.11 
 
Previous work on smoke particles from low-gravity sources by Urban et al. 5 indicated that the 
particulate produced by low-gravity fl ames (soot or unburned fuel partic les) tends to have larger size 
particles than in normal gravity. Results from the CSD (Comparative Soot Diagnostics) Experiment 5 
which studied smoke properties in low-gravity from several spacecraft materials suggested that liquid 
smoke particles could achieve sizes larger than 1 µm while solid particulate remained in the sub-
micrometer range. However, the CSD experiment di d not produce sufficient data concerning the size of 
the liquid smoke particles to guide detector design. The combined im pact of these lim ited results and 
physic

experiment di d not produce sufficient data concerning the size of 
the liquid smoke particles to guide detector design. The combined im pact of these lim ited results and 
physical expectations is that, ba sed on the increased sm oke residence time in low gravity, direct 
knowledge of low-g combustion partic ulate is needed for the confident design of smoke detectors for 
spacecraft rather than extrapolation from 1-g data 
 
Any effort to detect fires must be able to discriminate against the ambient background and nuisance 
signals. In the case of smoke detection, the background dust aerosol conditions must be considered. The 
only spacecraft background aerosol particulate measurem ents to date were made on the Orbiter on STS-
32 in 199012 and on the ISS.5

The STS measurements included the results from two cascade impactors and a light scattering device. 
The two impactors reported a bimodal particle size distribution with ~ 40% of the particles in each of the 
2.5 μm to 10 μm and >100 μm ranges. The other two ranges <2.5 μm and 10 μm to 100 μm were very 
lightly populated. Each impact or sampled approximately 15 m 3 of air over approximately 30 hours. 
These results showed substantially higher concentr ations than typical indoor measurements (over a 
factor of 5 for the two most populat ed size ranges). These data were supported by the li ght scattering 
instrument which made 17 measurements in 12 loca tions, all of these reported mass concentrations 
ranging from 50 μg/m3 to 70 μg/m3. The ISS results of Urban et al. 5 were obtained from a feasibility 
experiment to validate the operation of an aerosol particle counter in low-gravity (DAFT). The 
measurements were made in the US Lab on Increment 10 and the particle count levels were at the noise 
level for the instrument (less than 5 particles/cm 3). The low particle levels in th

passages.title: SAME Final Science Report
passages.text:
ements were made in the US Lab on Increment 10 and the particle count levels were at the noise 
level for the instrument (less than 5 particles/cm 3). The low particle levels in the < 2.5 μm bin for the 
STS and the low overall numbers for the ISS suggest a zone of opportunity for spacecraft fire detection 
since typical normal gravity fires produce su bstantial particulate in this size range 5,2 However more 
complete particle size statistics are needed. 
 
3. SAME Experiment 
 
To address the limited data from the CSD experime nt concerning the likely size of spacecraft smoke 
particulate, the Smoke Aerosol Measurement E xperiment (SAME) was developed. The SAME 
experiment sought to avoid the problems experi enced by the CSD experiment by obtaining the 
particulate size statistics on-orbit with a reduced dependence upon sample return to Earth. This is a 
challenging endeavor because existing aerosol instrumentation is typica lly too large to be compatible 
with spacecraft experiment constraints. Thus, to obtai n particulate size statistics with existing aerosol 
instrumentation wou

passages.title: SAME Final Science Report
passages.text:
umentation is typica lly too large to be compatible 
with spacecraft experiment constraints. Thus, to obtai n particulate size statistics with existing aerosol 
instrumentation would require the return of numerous samples to Earth. As will be described below, an 
alternative approach was employed that used three discrete instruments to measure separate moments of 
the size distribution. When combine d, these moments provide useful a ggregate statistics of the size 
distribution if a lognormal distri bution is assumed. The measurem ents were made using smoke 
generated by overheated spacecraft materials in much the same manner as the CSD experiment however 
the sample temperature, flow field, and particle aging time were more rigorously controlled. 
A. The Moment Method 
 
The approach used by the SAME experiment is termed the ‘moment method’ for convenience. 13 This 
approach consists of measuring three moments of the size distribution (the zeroth, first and third moment) 
on orbit, using several small, light -weight instruments. By applyi ng the properties of the lognormal 
distribu

on orbit, using several small, light -weight instruments. By applyi ng the properties of the lognormal 
distribution to the measured moments, the total number concentration, Nt, the geometric mean diameter, 
Dg, and the geometric standard deviation, g, of the aerosol can be estimated. Once these three 
parameters are known, the size distribution of the m easured aerosol is uniquely defined, assuming that 
the distribution is lognormal. In what follows, we will explain how the moment method works.

or integrated diameter per unit volume. The third moment, M3, is proportional, but not equal, to the total 
volume or mass of the particles per unit volume of the aerosol. From these three moments, two

denoted by D1.5 or md . The subscripts of 0.5 and 1.5 used for these two diameters follow an existing 
naming convention.

2.2 SAME Experiment Background 
Since the very beginning of the manned space flight program, NASA engineers and scientists have gone to great lengths to 
prevent fires from occurring on spacecraft. They have done this by adapting fire safety systems and procedures developed 
on Earth to the unique conditions and operating environment of spacecraft. However, microgravity combustion experiments 
have shown that fire can behave very differently in space and the best methods to prevent, detect, and extinguish fires on a 
spacecraft may be very different than those used on Earth. 
In 2000, NASA's Bioastronautics Initiative began with the objective of ensuring and enhancing the health, safety, and 
performance of humans in space. As part of this effort, the Life Support and Habitation Branch at NASA Glenn Research 
Center is responsible for developing and implementing a research plan to significantly improve fire safety on spacecraft and 
in space habitats. This goal will be achieved by applying a significant amount of fundamental knowledge and the 
experimental ca

passages.title: SAME Baseline Concept Description Doc
passages.text:
ignificantly improve fire safety on spacecraft and 
in space habitats. This goal will be achieved by applying a significant amount of fundamental knowledge and the 
experimental capability of microgravity research to spacecraft fire safety questions. 
Spacecraft smoke detectors must detect smoke with a variety of particulate types. Hydrocarbon fuels typically produce soot, 
while overheated plastics produce droplets of recondensed polymer fragments. Paper and silicone rubber produce a smoke 
that is composed of liquid droplets of recondensed pyrolysis products. Differences in the nucleation and growth processes 
for these different types of smokes create particles that have different sizes and properties. 
The Comparative Soot Diagnostics (CSD) experiment that flew in the Glovebox on STS-75 demonstrated that the smokes 
with solid particulates created in microgravity formed longer chains, and aggregated into larger particles than those created 
in normal Earth gravity. This is surmised to have occurred because of the increased residence time in the high concentration 
smoke regions a

passages.title: SAME Baseline Concept Description Doc
passages.text:
o larger particles than those created 
in normal Earth gravity. This is surmised to have occurred because of the increased residence time in the high concentration 
smoke regions and to have affected the responses of the two spacecraft smoke detectors (ISS and STS) utilized in that 
experiment. 
To develop smoke detectors that are sensitive to the type and size of smoke particles that will be encountered in 
microgravity and to allow them to distinguish between dust and smoke, better knowledge of the size distribution and 
morphology of the particulates is required. 
2.3 SAME Experiment Objectives 
The major goal of this experiment is to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulates achieve in microgravity and to 
relate the droplet size and distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment. This will 
be accomplished by extending the Comparative Soot Diagnostics (CSD) concept to provide a particulate count and mass 
density determination to the diagnostic array used to analyze these liquid smokes. The experimental design and practical 
app

passages.title: SAME Baseline Concept Description Doc
passages.text:
(CSD) concept to provide a particulate count and mass 
density determination to the diagnostic array used to analyze these liquid smokes. The experimental design and practical 
application of this data will be enhanced by the development of a numerical code that will predict the smoke droplet growth 
as a function of the fuel pyrolysis rate, the thermodynamic properties of the pyrolysis vapor, and the flow environment. 
The SAME experiment has the following (listed) objectives: 
1. Make measurements of three moments of the particle size distribution for the μg smoke from several 
materials found in spacecraft considering the effects of sample temperature, air flow, smoke residence time 
(near the source) and smoke aging. The primary targets are materials that produce liquid smoke particulate 
but solid smoke producers will also be considered. 
2. Make measurements of the effect of µg and 1-g on the size distribution of liquid aerosol smokes (using an 
idealized smoke e.g. DBT) to provide data for numerical model comparison. 
3. Evaluate the performance in µg of the two existing U.S.

passages.title: SAME Baseline Concept Description Doc
passages.text:
tribution of liquid aerosol smokes (using an 
idealized smoke e.g. DBT) to provide data for numerical model comparison. 
3. Evaluate the performance in µg of the two existing U.S. spacecraft smoke detector designs for the test 
conditions. 
4. Evaluate other smoke detection/sensing devices at NASA’s request for the test materials 
2.4 SAME “Firsts” for NASA 
• Measurements of microgravity smoke: Diagnostics such as the P-Trak and the DustTrak will be used to measure 
particle count and particle mass concentration, respectively. Both devices are manufactured by TSI. With the aid of 
these instruments (and others), microgravity smoke will be characterized. 
• The use of rapid prototype materials for manned flight experiment hardware. 
• Use of an automatic, remotely adjustable, ‘particulate friendly’ dilution system.

2.5 The SAME Risk mitigation experiment – DAFT 
The objective for the risk mitigation experiment, DAFT (Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test), is to provide a 
microgravity technology demonstration of the P-Trak Ultrafine Particle Counter manufactured by TSI. The P-Trak is a 
hand held air quality monitor which is capable of counting particles whose mean diameter is in the range of 1.0 to 0.05 
microns. 
After extensive market research performed by both the Engineering and Science teams, it has been determined that the P-
Trak is the only commercially available hardware that can perform this particle count while maintaining the weight, 
resource, and space limitations for an MSG experiment. 
P-Trak measures particle number concentrations in real-time while storing that data in a memory maintained by an on-
board battery. These measurements are made in units of particles per cubic centimeter (pt/cm3) versus traditional aerosol 
measurements of milligrams per cubic meter (mg/m3) made by photometers. P-Trak operates by using the particles in the 
aeroso

passages.title: SAME Baseline Concept Description Doc
passages.text:
cubic centimeter (pt/cm3) versus traditional aerosol 
measurements of milligrams per cubic meter (mg/m3) made by photometers. P-Trak operates by using the particles in the 
aerosol as seeds to condense droplets of alcohol (a condensate nuclei counter). These droplets have many times the average 
diameter of the original particles, and may, therefore, be easily counted with standard optical techniques. The potential 
problem is that these droplets are directed through a nozzle to facilitate the counting, and some of these droplets (a 
predictable percentage) collide with the walls and form a film. In a gravity environment, this film is recycled by ‘falling’ 
down hill. 
In microgravity, the distinct possibility exists that these droplets will form a film that will bridge and block the nozzle, 
effectively plugging the flow of droplets and preventing the device from functioning, or obscuring the optics. Furthermore, 
there is some concern that the droplets inside the optics chamber may get trapped in an internal circular motion and be 
counted more than once, producing an erroneously

passages.title: SAME Baseline Concept Description Doc
passages.text:
hermore, 
there is some concern that the droplets inside the optics chamber may get trapped in an internal circular motion and be 
counted more than once, producing an erroneously high count. 
The modification that was implemented in order to counteract these potential problems was: 60. 0.006” grooves were 
machined down the length of the inside of the condenser. These grooves were designed to provide a mechanism in which 
the smoke particle/ alcohol mixture can wick its way back to reservoir end to simulate the effects of gravity, hence, 
inhibiting the possibility of the fluid to inhibit the functioning of the unit. 
The modifications to account for and eliminate this problem have been devised and implemented, however, it is not possible 
to test the effectiveness of these modifications in any of the available ground based facilities and/or the KC-135 due to the 
duration of the nominal operation time required (minutes per instance). This testing, and the verification of the accuracy of 
the instrument functions on orbit, are the core of the DAFT experiment. 
Two P-Trak units are i

passages.title: SAME Baseline Concept Description Doc
passages.text:
uired (minutes per instance). This testing, and the verification of the accuracy of 
the instrument functions on orbit, are the core of the DAFT experiment. 
Two P-Trak units are included in DAFT flight hardware, one being only flight hardened, and the other with the modified 
condenser and flight hardened. 
To successfully accomplish P-Trak functional demonstration, additional hardware (which will not be explained in detail 
here) has to be delivered to the ISS. This hardware includes a dust concentration monitor (DustTrak), data cables, fill 
assembly, sample bag assemblies, sample holders, virtual impactor, alcohol reservoir, battery packs, a HEPA filter 
assembly, and appropriate tubing. 
The P-Trak utilizes isopropyl alcohol as a condensate, and its use must therefore, be carefully monitored and requires a 
specific agreement for that use on the ISS which is contained within a Volatile Usage Agreement (VUA) created for the 
experiment.

4.0 SAME CREW INTERFACES 
4.1 Hardware Subsystem Description 
The major planned components of SAME are as follows. They are organized by the assembly level, and the order in which 
they are currently planned to be installed into the MSG.: 
1. Fluids Control Box Assembly (67198MABA220) 
The Fluids Control Box (FCB) installs on the back wall of the MSG in the upper left section. It is a fan cooled 
enclosure made from aluminum that contains most of the fluids control devices and monitoring devices including 
solenoids, pressure r

passages.title: SAME Baseline Concept Description Doc
passages.text:
in the upper left section. It is a fan cooled 
enclosure made from aluminum that contains most of the fluids control devices and monitoring devices including 
solenoids, pressure regulator, pressure transducers and mass flow controller. It interfaces directly with the MSG 
fluids resources (VES and GN2) and the Power Distribution and Control Unit (PDCU), and distributes the fluids 
resources accordingly. Please refer to the SAME Fluids Schematic (67198PABA000) for more information on its, 
and the other fluids system functions. 
2. Sample Plate Assembly (Experiment Support Plate Assembly) 67198ABA100 
This assembly, when fully integrated, contains all of the major functional systems of SAME. It is a mounting plate 
which includes the mounting hardware for the Sample Carousel, the Thermal Precipitator Unit (TPU), the 
Dynamic Diagnostics Assembly (DDA) and the Aging Chamber Assembly (ACA). Permanently mounted to it 
are: 
• The Smoke Generation Tube 
• The Video Camera and Controller 
• The Sample Positioning system including: 
o the Sample Turning Module 
o the sample engagement mech

are: 
• The Smoke Generation Tube 
• The Video Camera and Controller 
• The Sample Positioning system including: 
o the Sample Turning Module 
o the sample engagement mechanism 
o the sample position indicator 
o the sample positioning lock mechanism 
o the Sample Carousel mounting system

passages.title: SAME Baseline Concept Description Doc
passages.text:
SAME-DOC-001 Rev. A

3. Dynamic Diagnostics Assembly (DDA) (67198MDBA165) 
The DDA is attached to the Sample Plate Assembly and the Aging Chamber Assembly by the crew and contains: 
the ISS and STS smoke detectors and the sampling ports that supply the P-Trak Enclosure and the Commercial 
Diagnostics Enclosure (and port(s) added for any additional diagnostics required). The DDA has a very low 
internal volume, and the flow of the sample aerosol through it is controlled by regulating and balancing the 
requirements of the active diagnostics in the DDA with the exhaust rate of the Aging Chamber piston, as 
controlled by its mass flow controller. It also contains a port, protected by a HEPA filter, that is connected to the 
VES for exhaust and purging. 
4. Aging Chamber Assembly (67198MABA150) 
The Aging Chamber Assembly contains the cylindrical, metallic Aging Chamber, the pneumatically activated 
Inlet and Outlet Gate Valves and the Inlet and Outlet Elbows, which connect to the Smoke Generation Tube and 
the DDA, respectively. A Rulon piston, internal to the chamber, moves the sam

passages.title: SAME Baseline Concept Description Doc
passages.text:
nd Outlet Gate Valves and the Inlet and Outlet Elbows, which connect to the Smoke Generation Tube and 
the DDA, respectively. A Rulon piston, internal to the chamber, moves the sample into and out from the internal 
volume, and that flow is controlled by a mass flow controller which regulates the pressure or vacuum flow 
accordingly. Sampling ports are provided in the elbows for use by the Thermal Precipitator, and the unit contains 
a Mixing Fan to insure that the contents are homogenous before disbursal to the DDA. 
5. Data Acquisition and Control Unit (DACU) (67198EABA660) 
The DACU is the central control unit for SAME. The baseline software is resident there, and, although many of 
the other packages contain their own relay and control cards, ultimately it is the DACU that interfaces with the 
Ethernet and the MLC to orchestrate the performance of the experiment. It also collects and stores data for 
subsequent downlink through the MSG systems, and controls the MSG Video Recorder to provide a taped record 
of the pyrolysis event. 
6. P-Trak Enclosure (67198MABA500) 
The P-Trak En

passages.title: SAME Baseline Concept Description Doc
passages.text:
bsequent downlink through the MSG systems, and controls the MSG Video Recorder to provide a taped record 
of the pyrolysis event. 
6. P-Trak Enclosure (67198MABA500) 
The P-Trak Enclosure is a flight hardened assembly containing a TSI P-Trak modified to take advantage of the 
VES system and to function in a microgravity environment. Although it interfaces with the DDA, the DACU, the 
Fluids Control Unit and the Power Distribution and Control Unit, it is basically a smart box that can operate 
independently and store its own data. 
7. Commercial Diagnostics Enclosure (CDE) (67198MABA600) 
The CDE houses two of the SAME diagnostics, the TSI DustTrak and a First Alert ionization smoke detector. 
Both units have been hardened for flight and have been modified to utilize the VES to drive the sample. The 
DustTrak has also been modified to utilize MSG air to provide its ‘sheath air’ in order to decrease the amount of 
aerosol required by the unit. Like P-Trak, the DustTrak portion of this device can operate independently and store 
its own data. The modified First Alert cannot. 
8. Dynamic

passages.title: SAME Baseline Concept Description Doc
passages.text:
t of 
aerosol required by the unit. Like P-Trak, the DustTrak portion of this device can operate independently and store 
its own data. The modified First Alert cannot. 
8. Dynamic Diluter (DD) (67198MABA180) 
The DD is a custom designed component that provides dilution of the aerosol from the DDA before its 
introduction into the P-Trak (and possibly the DustTrak). It works by utilizing a laminar flow element to measure 
the amount of sample being introduced and using that information (from a differential pressure transducer) to 
increase or decrease the diluent flow to achieve the desired concentration. The dilution setpoint may be altered by 
software and adjusts to the desired setting in approximately 5 seconds. 
9. Power Distribution and Control Unit (PDCU) (67198EABA680) 
The PDCU is the central disbursement point for the commands, power distribution and data collection for SAME. 
It contains the power converters, main relays and terminal data connections for the entire system and interfaces the 
DACU with the various systems and devices constituting the experiment.

10. Sample Carousel Assembly (67198MABB400) 
The Sample Carousel Assemblies (5) each contain six (6) Sample Tubes that interface the samples to the Smoke 
Generation Tube and allow the capture of the smoke in the Aging Chamber. Sample Carousels are sequentially 
installed onto the mounting locations on the Sample Plate Assembly, and the mechanisms contained by it identify 
the individual sample numbers, rotate the carousel to the correct position and engage the Sample Tube, which 
allows the sample to be in a position to be energized. The samples themselves are composed of five (5) materials: 
Teflon, Kapton, Silicone, Cellulose and DiButyl Phthalate (which being a liquid, is contained within a small 
section of cotton lampwick) in small, cylindrical sections, that are wrapped with coils of wire (baseline: stainless 
steel) that both provides the heat energy to the sample when energized and measures its temperature (by its 
varying resistance). 
These samples are removed from the tubes for weighing, both before and after the experiment (before launch and 
aft

passages.text:
ized and measures its temperature (by its 
varying resistance). 
These samples are removed from the tubes for weighing, both before and after the experiment (before launch and 
after being downmassed) to quantify the actual mass loss during pyrolysis. 
11. Thermal Precipitator Unit (TPU) (67198MABB300) 
The TPU is a device that captures actual samples of the aerosol particulate on Transmission Electron Microscope 
(TEM) grids for examination when returned from the ISS. The units (4) are number matched to the samples in the 
carousel, to take samples from both the Inlet and Outlet Elbows leading to and from the Aging Chamber. 
12. Alcohol Wick Storage Container (67198MABD700) 
The Alcohol Wick Storage Container is a custom manufactured aluminum vessel to contain the alcohol wick 
required by the P-Trak during the time (launch, non-ops) when it is not in direct use. Only one is nominally 
required, but two are included to provide one as a backup. 
13. Hoses 
SAME utilizes ISS GN2 and the VES system both as resources for the experiment process and as systems to 
power its devices. These

passages.title: SAME Baseline Concept Description Doc
passages.text:
e included to provide one as a backup. 
13. Hoses 
SAME utilizes ISS GN2 and the VES system both as resources for the experiment process and as systems to 
power its devices. These resources are distributed to the components from the FCU via the hoses, which are 
nominally operated at +/- 15 psig. In order to conserve weight and volume, and provide ease of operation, acrylic 
hoses and quick disconnects will be used for the distribution of pressure and vacuum throughout the system (not 
typical Teflon with stainless steel overbraid). 
14. Harnessing 
All harnessing will conform to applicable standards and be designed to minimize the crew time needed to make 
the required experiment connections, without sacrificing reliability. 
15. SAME Service Kit 
This is a place holder. SAME has not yet defined any servicing requirements. 
4.2 Video Recording Devices 
Video recordings of the smoke evolution process are very important for establishing proper operation of the test apparatus 
and for debugging the system operation. Furthermore, the video provides a helpful demonstration of the variab

passages.title: SAME Baseline Concept Description Doc
passages.text:
ery important for establishing proper operation of the test apparatus 
and for debugging the system operation. Furthermore, the video provides a helpful demonstration of the variability in 
smoke evolution. Experience with CSD showed dramatic cases where clearly visible smoke streams were not always 
detectable by the smoke detectors while invisible smoke streams were readily detected. Normal video resolution is 
acceptable if the smoke is illuminated by forward scattered light from an appropriate light source. Video will be viewed on 
and recorded by the MSG video Monitor/Recorder. 
4.3 On-Orbit Crew Operational Functions 
The crew will be asked to assemble the experiment from provided subsections, load software, reload Sample Carousels, 
Thermal Precipitator Modules, and alcohol for the particle counter, enter parameters, initiate the experiment, and 
disassemble the experiment.

5.0 SAME SOFTWARE CONTROL 
5.1 Software Controlled Operational Functions 
The DACU is the central point for SAME control. It is ultimately responsible for all experiment operations and interfacing 
with the environment external to SAME. It contains all of the logic necessary to autonomously operate the experiment as 
well as receive, validate, and process commands from the MSG. The DACU periodically transmits the status of the Smoke 
system to the MSG, which then forwards it to the ground. The software can autonomously control the progress of 
preprogrammed test, manage and store all science and system files on the local data storage medium, control the MSG 
video recorder capturing Smoke images, and copy the files to the MLC for downlink. The software inside the DACU is 
also responsible for providing diagnostic information and manual control of all sensors and controls using the GSE port. 
Please refer to the SAME Baseline Software Requirements Document (SAME-DOC-004) for more detail. 
5.2 Data Collection 
Data is collected and stored in the DACU until it i

passages.title: SAME Baseline Concept Description Doc
passages.text:
SE port. 
Please refer to the SAME Baseline Software Requirements Document (SAME-DOC-004) for more detail. 
5.2 Data Collection 
Data is collected and stored in the DACU until it is time to downlink the information. The Thermal Precipitator Module, 
which collects samples of the smoke, will be bagged and returned for analysis. Sample Carousels are retained so that the 
samples can be weighed after return to Earth. 
6.0 SAME OPERATIONS 
6.1 Operations Flow 
1. Experiment Setup- The experiment will be shipped in individual subassemblies that will be assembled inside of 
the MSG. Parts will be inserted through the MSG side ports starting with the upper, back components. After 
the MSG ports are covered and the rack is returned to nominal position, the Experiment Software is installed 
onto the MSG Laptop. 
2. Perform Experiment- The first steps in performing the experiment are to load the desired Sample Carousel, load 
or replenish the alcohol wick in the particle counter, and install a new Thermal Precipitator Module. Next, the 
start-up check out routine is performed. After the uplink

passages.title: SAME Baseline Concept Description Doc
passages.text:
el, load 
or replenish the alcohol wick in the particle counter, and install a new Thermal Precipitator Module. Next, the 
start-up check out routine is performed. After the uplink parameters are sent, the experiment is initiated. Then, 
the baseline uplink parameters are modified, as required, for the next test and the experiment is initiated again 
until all six samples in the Sample Carousel have been used. The next number matched Sample Carousel and 
Thermal Precipitator Module will then be loaded and the experiment will continue as such until complete. 
3. Shutdown and Repack Experiment- When all the Sample Carousels have been used and all the experiments 
have been performed, the final Sample Carousel and Thermal Precipitator Module will be capped and bagged. 
In reverse order of installation, the experiment hardware will be repackaged for downmassing. 
6.2 Detailed Operations 
Please refer to the SAME Operations Concept Document (SAME-DOC-009) for a more detailed description of all 
Operations functions.

Since the experiment is designed for operations controlled from the ground, once the components have been installed in the

SAME will follow the standard ISS procedures for scheduling activities aboard the station including OCR and iURC

7.0 SAFETY CONCERNS & PREVENTATIVE MEASURES 
7.1 Overall Strategy 
Safety analysis is being performed for the SAME (formerly Smoke) hardware in accordance with the safety policies and 
safety requirements for flight hardware (NSTS1700.7B and ISS Addendum). This assessment is being prepared using 
NSTS 13830C as a guideline for data submittal. Hazards not eliminated by design are addressed in either the latest revision 
of standardized hazard contro

of standardized hazard control report JSC Form 1230 for ISS and launch/landing phase of the mission or in a Unique 
Hazard Report, JSC 542B. For the most part, the SAME experiment uses generic hazard controls for electrical power 
hazards, sharp edges, EMI (testing), rotating equipment (smaller than 8 inch diameter rotors and less than 8000 RPM), Fire

2.0 IN-FLIGHT FUNCTIONAL CHECKLIST 
This is a list of items that should be addressed after the hardware is installed in the MSG and before any 
samples are tested. Not currently in any order. 
- Perform piston calibration and alter registry values as necessary. See procedure later in this 
document. Run a test with heater setpoint below R0 and no use of the thermal precipitors in order 
to confirm correct calibration. 
- Figure out good values for STSPumpFailureLowLimit and STSPumpFailureHighLimit registry 
values. These depend somewhat on atmospheric pressure and should be adjusted for the ISS 
environment. Correctly set, these values help detect failure of the STS pump. 
- Log some data with the P-Trak and DustTrak and confirm that their settings are correct. For 
example: log interval, time constant, and date/time. 
- Record some video, downlink, and examine. 
- Experimentally determine the maximum setpoints that the mass flow controller will meet given 
ISS vacuum and GN2 sources. Determine if any desired inlet velocities or diagnostic 
combinations are affecte

ISS vacuum and GN2 sources. Determine if any desired inlet velocities or diagnostic 
combinations are affected. 
- The registry value, DisableChecksumCheck, can be set to 1 to avoid the startup delay associated 
with calculating the checksum each time. 
- Revisit the decision about whether the heater controller offset correction will be done 
automatically as part of the test sequence or manually using the HeaterCorrectOffset utility prior 
to the test sequence. Adjust the CorrectOffset registry value appropriately.

4.0 TEST CHECKLIST 
This is a list of important things to do or confirm pr ior to, during, and after the running of a sample test. 
Placement of a highly visible printout of this lis t on console is recommended. Steps depend on whether 
sample heater offset correction is being done automatically or manually. Check the CorrectOffset registry 
value to find out (0=manual, >0=automatic). 
- Once per carousel open the gate valves and turn on the diagnostics for TBD minutes. Downlink 
the data and verify correctness. The purpose is to collect baseline measurements of the MSG work 
volume required by the science team. 
4.1 With Automatic Heater Offset Correction 
- Power on the system, wait for telemetry reception. 
- Send the Initialize command. 
- If the desired sample is not engaged, engage it using the Self Test command. 
- Turn on the 12VDC Heater Power. 
- Note the sample resistance and compare to ground measured resistance. If they differ

significantly, TBD. Determine the setpoint.

sample number must be correct. 
- Start the test. 
- When the test pauses check the following: 
o A “sample type is confirmed” message appears in the log. 
o The offset correction returned a value less than 50uV in the log. 
o The sample resistance is still good. Within TBD % of before. 
o The desired diagnostics are powered and readings are nominal. 
o GN2 regulated pressure and vacuum pressure are good. Range is TBD.

still greater than 50uV, change the CorrectOffset registry value to 0 (manual) and use the manual

- Resume the test.

an Abort command. 
- Watch the sample resistance and compare to the desired setpoint and MaxRt. The sof

on the 12 VDC Heater Enable (right click on the ‘ LED’ and select ‘Set On’). Sample Resistance will 
settle to a valid measurement within 4 seconds. 
5.3 Registry File Concerns 
Assuming you’ve set the test parameters to a specif ic carousel number, sample number, heating setpoint 
and duration, you may think you are ready to go. Y ou may not be. There are a bunch of sample-related 
limit checks that may cause an error or warning prior to heating. There are also many timing constants 
that affect the system behavior. These can be cha nged by selecting Set Registry… on the System tab. 
See SAME-DOC-005, Software Interface Control Document for key names and descriptions. A system 
timing simulator, currently located in SAMEFluidMode l.xls, will be available on console to help see the 
effect of registry value changes. Testing with the engineering unit is also recommended. 
A

currently located in SAMEFluidMode l.xls, will be available on console to help see the 
effect of registry value changes. Testing with the engineering unit is also recommended. 
Alternately, registry values can be changed by editing the registry.txt file on the DACU. This file is 
located in the /config directory. Also in that dir ectory is registry.orig.txt which contains the original 
registry settings. 
Important: Changes to registry values will not take e ffect until you restart the software. Follow the 
steps for shutting down, below, but use the restart parameter option.

5.4 Running the Test 
From the Testing tab select Start… and enter the test number to run, if it hasn’t already been entered in 
the field, and select Send. 
After sample positioning and aging chamber setup has occurred the test will pause so you can examine 
the log for any warnings or errors. Then send the Resume button. The test should proceed to finish. You 
can abort anytime by sending the Abort command. An abort causes all valves to be turned off as well as 
all diagnostics. 
5.5 Shutdown 
It is recommended that the system be gracefully shut down using the Shutdown button on the System tab, 
then cut power about 2 minutes later. Current housek eeping and log files are transferred to the laptop 
during the first minute. Use the second minute to ensu re that the system did not restart, looking for the 
restart of low rate telemetry packets and updating GMT. If the system restarts, select Shutdown again or 
send the OS command with parameter, ‘/bin/shutdown –b’. 
5.6 Self-Tests 
The flight software has a few operations available through the SelfTest command. The

5.6 Self-Tests 
The flight software has a few operations available through the SelfTest command. These may be useful 
for other than self-test purposes, for instance to engage a sample to the inlet tube to check R0. Parameters 
depend on the self test:

6.0 PROCESSING FILES 
6.1 Transferring files from DACU to the MLC 
All files will be automatically transferred from th e DACU to C:\ftp on the MSG laptop. Housekeeping 
files (.hkp) are transferred on the hour and upon shut down (with either the shutdown or restart option). 
The Log file is also transferred upon shutdown. P- Trak, DustTrak, and heater files are transferred soon 
after they are created. P-Trak and DustTrak file s are not automatically created since their data is 
embedded in the housekeeping data. To explicitly retrie ve logged data select the Transfer Data button on 
the DustTrak and P-Trak tabs. This should be do ne no more frequently than once per minute because the 
filename is derived from the GMT, including the latest minute, but not the latest second. 
If you need the data immediately or a file doesn’t get downlinked for some reason you’ll have to do it 
manually using one of two methods described here: 
6.1.1 Using SAMEDisplay and FTP Cmd command. 
You’ll need to identify what file you need and the dir ectory it is in. Files are stored in a

6.1.1 Using SAMEDisplay and FTP Cmd command. 
You’ll need to identify what file you need and the dir ectory it is in. Files are stored in a directory named 
according to GMT year and day. For instance /data/2006_132/. The .log file will be named 
2006_132_00.log in this example. Housekeeping files will be 2006_132_15.hkp, 2006_132_16.hkp, etc. 
according to the GMT. 
With the flight software and SAMEDisplay running (does not need to be Initialized), select the FTP Cmd 
from the System tab. Type: LCD /data/2006_132, for example, to change local directory (on the DACU) 
and send the command. Then select FTP Cmd again a nd type: PUT 2006_132_16.hkp, for example, and 
send the command. Watch your letter case – it matters. 
6.1.2 Using SAME processor command line to transfer files 
For this to work you’ll need a keyboard and mon itor connected to the GSE port on the SAME DACU. 
Also, verify that the switch on the SAME DACU is sw itched to Override position. This is obviously a 
ground use only method. 
From the command line on the GSE monitor (if th

From the command line on the GSE monitor (if the so ftware is running you can get another console

7.0 MISCELLANEOUS PROCEDURES AND INFORMATION 
7.1 Obtaining a directory listing 
An example: 
- OSCommand(‘ls –l /data/2006_237 > /data/dir.txt’). 
- FTPCommand(‘LCD /data’). 
- FTPCommand(‘PUT dir.txt’). 
- Have MSG cadre downlink the file dir.txt. 
7.2 Replacing the registry file 
Normally you would change individual entries usi ng the SetRegistry command. This method could be 
used to set the registry to a known state, perhaps a f ile under source control, using an uplinked file. And 
this is the only way I could get the copied-over registry.txt file to ‘take’. If the system is shut down nicely 
through the shutdown command then it appears to revert to the old registry file. 
 - FTPCommand(‘LCD /config’). 
 - FTPCommand(‘GET registry.new.txt’) 
 - OSCommand(‘cp /config/registry.txt /config/registry.old.txt’) 
 - OSCommand(‘cp /config/registry.new.txt /config/registry.txt’) 
 - Do a hard shutdown: power off 
 - Power on and the new settings should take effect. 
7.3 Piston Calibration

7.3 Piston Calibration 
Piston calibration, a.k.a. piston characterization, is a process of adjusting some registry values so that 
piston rates and time marks are correct for current conditions. This process should be performed 
whenever there is a change of hardware, especially the aging chamber and piston itself; a change of 
environment, such as the move to the ISS; a change of fluid source strength; or a change of hardware 
condition, perhaps after many tests have been run. 
7.3.1 Inlet Velocity 
Actual inlet velocity is required to match desired inle t velocity to within +/- 0.5 cm/sec. Actual velocity 
is not a directly measured value. It is a function of piston bottom to top travel time, chamber volume, and 
inlet tube diameter. The equation is:

7.3.2 Sample Heating Start Time 
Ideally, the start of sample heating is calculated so that the end of sample heating occurs before the piston 
reaches the top of the chamber. Actually, even before that, so that most of the smoke in the inlet tube at 
the end of heating enters the chamber as well. And really, even before that, so that some clean air follows 
the ‘last’ of the smoke and more of the smoke enters the chamber. The amount of the latter clean air is 
determined by the BackEndCleanAirOffset registry value. 
Because there is no direct physical measurement of where the piston is in the middle of its stroke, the 
software must estimate when the stroke begins and how long the stroke will take. Then it can back off 
from there to determine sample heating sto

7.3.3 Secondary Aging Volume 
When a secondary aging period and volume are speci fied, the piston must stop a percentage of the 
distance between the top and bottom of the chamber. There is no direct physical measurement of the 
running distance, therefore it is estimated from th e exhaust rate over time. The registry value, 
ExhaustPercentageCorrectionFactor, is applied to the running percentage. To adjust this value, 
- Perform a SelfTest to exhaust the chamber to a specific percentage. For best results use the 
exhaust rate and secondary volume that will be used during the actual test. Or use 5 LPM and 
50%. 
- Perform a SelfTest to exhaust the chamber the rest of the way. Use the same rate and 100%. 
- Calculate the time taken for each portion using log messages or pressure data and figure the 
percentage of total time taken by the second exhaust. Adjust the registry value and repeat until 
this percentage is within the desired accuracy of the secondary aging volume percentage. 
7.3.4 Exhaust Rate 
It was verified that the system exhausts at a rate sufficient

until 
this percentage is within the desired accuracy of the secondary aging volume percentage. 
7.3.4 Exhaust Rate 
It was verified that the system exhausts at a rate sufficient to achieve overpressure of the diagnostic duct 
for all combinations of diagnostic use except when usi ng the STS detector with both DustTraks. If this 
situation changes, the exhaust rate can be increased using the ExhaustOverpressureRate registry value. 
7.4 Changing flight software during flight 
Description: Transfer new version of flight software from MLC to DACU. Uses crew time, SAME 
Utility Cable, and HyperTerminal application on MLC to perform ftp transfer, backup old flight software, 
and replace it with the new. Reboots are necessary b ecause the software runs au tomatically on startup 
and cannot be replaced while running. Therefore, afte r making a backup, the software is removed so that 
it cannot autostart. Then the new version is copied to the autostart name. Upon reboot, the system finds 
the autostart name again, the new version of software, and operation proceeds normally.

ABSTRACT 
 
 
 
 
Title of Document: SMOKE POINTS OF MICROGRAVITY AND 
NORMAL GRAVITY COFLOW DIFFUSION 
FLAMES 
 
 Keenan Thomas Dotson, M.S., 2009 
 
Directed By: Assistant Professor, Peter B. Sunderland, 
Department of Fire Protection Engineering 
 
 
Smoke points were measured in microgravity aboard the International Space Station 
(ISS) as part of the Smoke Points in Coflow Experiment (SPICE), and in normal 
gravity conditions. In microgravity conditions increasing the coflow velocity or 
decreasing the burner diameter increased the smoke point flame length. A simplified 
prediction of centerline jet velocity did not yield residence-time-based criticalities or 
data collapse. Simulation of non-reacting flows showed that the simplified centerline 
velocity prediction was able to predict velocity decay for only relatively weak 
coflows. An improved model may yield different results. In normal earth gravity 
coflow velocity exhibited mixed effects. For burner diameters of 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 
mm, smoke points increased with increases of coflow velocity. For an unconfined 
coflow bur

coflow velocity exhibited mixed effects. For burner diameters of 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 
mm, smoke points increased with increases of coflow velocity. For an unconfined 
coflow burner with a burner diameter of 13.7 mm smoke point length decreased with 
increasing coflow velocity for ethylene and propylene, while increasing for propane 
flames.

Chapter 1. Introduction 
Soot formation is an important but unresolved problem in combustion science. In 
many circumstances soot production in flames is desired. Nevertheless, once soot 
escapes the flame and becomes smoke, it is rarely if ever wanted in a combustion 
system. Soot is estimated to be responsible for up to 52,000 premature deaths in the 
U.S. 1 and is believed to contribute to climate change and glacial melting. 2 Radiation 
from soot in flames allows reading by candlelight, provides heat to campers, and 
cooks our food. On the other hand this radiation can represent a loss of efficiency and 
increased heat loads in engines. Also the spread of unwanted fires is in many cases is 
through the radiation heat transfer originating from soot particles. Smoking flames 
emit carbon monoxide, which is the major cause of death in fires. 3 
 
1.1. Smoke Point 
The laminar smoke point is the condition (or luminous flame length) where a laminar 
diffusion flame begins to emit soot. Smoke points are the prevalentmethod used to 
determine fuel sooting propensity in diffusion fl

passages.text:
ion (or luminous flame length) where a laminar 
diffusion flame begins to emit soot. Smoke points are the prevalentmethod used to 
determine fuel sooting propensity in diffusion flames. The longer the luminous 
(visible) flame length at its smoke point, the lower the sooting propensity of the fuel. 
In normal gravity, laminar smoke points have been measured for many gaseous and 
condensed fuels. 4,5,6,7,8,9 Laminar smoke points have been found to correlate with soot 
volume fractions 10 and radiative loss fractions 11 of turbulent diffusion flames. Yang et 
al. 12 found that gas turbine soot emissions correlate with a threshold sooting index 
(TSI) based on fuel molecular weight divided by the laminar smoke point. Smoke 
points have been shown to correlate with the smoke release from turbulent buoyant 
 4 -6, 7 -9

passages.id: PSI-107::PSI-107_Reports_SMOKE POINTS OF MICROGRAVITY AND  NORMAL GRAVITY COFLOW DIFFUSION  FLAMES_DotsonThesis.pdf::p12::24

flames, 13 and have been applied to developing general soot models for computation 
combustion simulations 14 and heat release measurements. 15 
 
Smoke points for gaseous fuels are determined from a jet flame apparatus. A 
surrounding coflow of excess oxidant (over-ventilated conditions) is typically 
necessary for buoyant flames to reduce flame flickering. It is also most common to 
confine the coflow and jet within a quartz chimney to reduce disturbances from 
exterior flows. Shorter smoke point flame lengths are indicative of a higher sooting 
propensity. A flame that has a lower inclination to form soot will exhibit a smoke free 
flame for longer flame lengths; that is longer flame residence times are required to 
create the necessary amount of soot to reach the smoke point condition. 
 
1.2. Soot Formation, Growth, and Oxidation 
General consensus has that the soot formation process begins with the formation of 
polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs). From these precursors fine soot particles 
nucleate. These particles grow by addition of PAHs or through surface reactions

passages.text:
he formation of 
polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs). From these precursors fine soot particles 
nucleate. These particles grow by addition of PAHs or through surface reactions. The 
Hydrogen Abstraction by Carbon (Acetylene) Addition (HACA) mechanism is one of 
the most often cited for soot growth mechanisms. In addition, coagulation, in which 
small particles coalesce into larger particles and agglomeration, where multiple 
particles combine into larger pearl-necklace-like structures, also contribute to 
morphology. Soot oxidation occurs from participation from species such as O 2, O, 
and OH present near and downstream of the flame sheet. OH-based oxidation is the 
most dominant soot oxidation mechanism, occurring from slightly rich to lean

conditions within the flame. O 2-based oxidation becomes more important as the flame 
becomes leaner and the super-equilibrium levels of OH decline.16 Both soot formation 
and soot oxidation are temperature dependent. 
 
Detailed measurements have provided greater insight into sooting phenomena. In 
premixed ethylene flames, Harris and Weiner 17,18 determined that soot reaches a final 
particle size due to a decrease in reactivity of the particle that stops surface growth, 
and the dominate growth mechanism is by acetylene. In diffusion flames Kent et 
al. 19,20 have shown that soot particles are formed primarily on the fuel side of the 
flame reaction zone. The number of particles decreases by coagulation away from the 
peak formation zone (a few millimeters inside the reaction zone on the fuel side), 
while particle size and soot volume fraction increase by the addition of hydrocarbon 
species. Soot typically convects towards the fuel side of the flame after it has formed 
from buoyancy. The soot path ultimately follows on the local streamlines.

from buoyancy. The soot path ultimately follows on the local streamlines. 
Thermophoretic forces modify these paths slightly towards cooler regions within the 
flame. 
 
Santoro et al. 21,22 discovered a unique feature of coflow diffusion flames. The 
annular region near the base of the flame is a location of intense nucleation and 
agglomeration of soot. This formation region is the cause of the soot 'wings' seen in 
diffusion flames near their smoke points. Gomez et al. 23 found that soot formation 
begins at a temperature around 1350 K in diffusion flames and that dilution does not 
change this temperature but rather shifts the location at which this temperature

occurs. Sunderland and Faeth 24 determined soot nucleation to become significant at 
1250 K. Kent and Wagner 25 found that smoke burnout in the oxidative region of the 
flame ceases when the tip of a buoyant diffusion flame cools to approximately 
1300 K. This is the direct cause of the smoke point flame. Urban et al. 26 found that 
the luminous tip of a nonbuoyant (microgravity) flame reaches 1000 K at its smoke 
point. In buoyant flames this decrease in temperature is attributed primarily to heat 
conduction, and in nonbuoyant flames this can be significantly enhanced by radiative 
quenching. 16 Radiative quenching is believed to also cause the visible tip opening in 
nonbuoyant smoke points of flames of relatively long residence times.26 
 
In diffusion flames, oxygen and fuel meet at a narrow reaction zone, the flame sheet. 
Kinetics does not determine the location or temperature of this zone, but rather 
stoichiometry does. Diffusion limits the flow of the reactants to this narrow flame 
sheet and, for strong flames, is much slower than the kinetic reaction rate. 
Furthermo

rather 
stoichiometry does. Diffusion limits the flow of the reactants to this narrow flame 
sheet and, for strong flames, is much slower than the kinetic reaction rate. 
Furthermore the soot formation/oxidation times are believed to be greater than the 
time necessary for diffusion of reactants. 27 If chemical kinetics is practically 
instantaneous, then residence time becomes the determining factor for soot formation 
and oxidation. It has also been suggested that the ratio of soot formation and soot 
oxidation times also determines when the smoke point will occur. Lautenberger et 
al. 27 describe this process for buoyant laminar flames. “Increasing the flame height 
increases the residence time and allows more time for the flame to produce soot. 
Once formed, this soot requires additional time to oxidize in the upper parts of the

flame if it is to be entirely consumed below the flame tip. As soot travels through the 
flame (in a Lagrangian sense), it radiates away energy and cools the flame gases.” 
Also corroborating what was mentioned previously about a limiting temperature at 
which soot oxidation ceases, typically at the smoke point flame height, the radiative 
heat loss from the flame by soot radiation is about 30% of the total heat release rate of 
the flame. 28 The cooled flame gases can no longer oxidize the soot and one could 
consider the soot formation/oxidation time to approach the diffusion time. 27 Smoke is 
then released from the tip of this flame and it has just surpassed its characteristic 
smoke point because the required time for soot oxidation is now less than the time the 
soot is capable of being oxidized post flame sheet. 
 
Important review articles on soot formation mechanisms are available from 
Frenklach 29 , Mansurov 30 , and Glassman.31 Richter and Howard 32 in a particularly 
detailed fashion reviewed the formation of PAHs and their growth to soot. Soot 
oxidation is well co

1.3. Fuel and Diluent Effects 
For diffusion flames, work by Schalla and McDonald 34 showed that fuel sooting 
propensity decreases with hydrocarbon family in the following order: aromatics > 
alkynes > alkenes> alkanes. According to Glassman 31 , increasing the molecular 
weight of the fuel increases the soot formation rate by increasing the radical 
concentration and the Arrhenius pre-exponential factor for the overall rate coefficient. 
In premixed flames, the number of carbon-carbon (C-C) bonds determines the critical

is only an indirect measure of the pyrolysis rate of the fuel. 
 
In diffusion flames H radicals are important to the fuel pyrolysis process, facilitating 
the initial pyrolysis of the virgin fuel as well as the subsequent attack on fuel 
intermediates. H radicals facilitate abstraction reactions much faster than hydrocarbon 
radicals do. Despite this importance of H radicals, Schug et al. 4 have shown that the 
initial overall carbon-hydrogen (C/H) atom ratio of the fuel does not determine the 
sooting propensity. Nevertheless the degree of molecular unsaturation correlates with 
higher sooting propensity, perhaps likely due to the greater ease these molecules can 
form acetylenes and PAHs. 
 
In over-ventilated coflow diffusion flames, addition of inert to the fuel stream 
typically reduces sooting propensity. Longer smoke points result. However the 
addition of inert can also alter the flame temperature. This occurs by the inert acting 
as a heat sink, this effect depending on the heat capac

addition of inert can also alter the flame temperature. This occurs by the inert acting 
as a heat sink, this effect depending on the heat capacity of the inert.4,35 The peak 
flame temperatures will be reduced, which for a diffusion flame reduces soot 
formation, increasing the smoke point. Additionally, the temperature field of the 
flame can be altered through transport effects. Inert species with high thermal 
diffusivities have their volumetric dilution effects countered by a thermal effect of 
extending the high temperature range where soot formation is possible. 36 The 
temperature of the pyrolysis zone determines the soot propensity and correlates well

the fuel mass flow rate at the smoke height. Shock tube experiments have shown that 
the soot formation rate peaks around 1900 – 2300 K.31 
 
1.4. Buoyancy Effects 
Soot is transported in flames primarily by convection, modified slightly by 
thermophoresis. The primary difference between a buoyant and nonbuoyant jet 
flames is that, in general, a buoyant flame, the flow is accelerating, while for a 
nonbuoyant jet the flow is decelerating. This is of course neglecting volumetric 
expansion from combustion related heating. In general, for a buoyant flame the flow 
streamlines move towards the flame axis, while for the nonbuoyant flame the flow 
streamlines are drawn outwards from the flame axis.16 Therefore in a buoyant flame, 
once soot is nucleated in the soot production region near the flame sheet, it is drawn 
into the fuel rich core, allowing continued growth. In a nonbuoyant flame as the flow 
is drawn outwards, the soot moves in a more direct path to the flame sheet and 
oxidative region downstream. 16 
 
It had been predicted that smoke points would not occur in nonbuoyan

oxidative region downstream. 16 
 
It had been predicted that smoke points would not occur in nonbuoyant gas-jet 
flames. 37 This was based on the assumption that residence time would be independent 
of flow rate in microgravity flames. As flame length and mass flow rate are directly 
proportional, an increase in velocity would lead to proportional increase in length and 
residence time would remain unchanged. In normal gravity flames the residence time 
scales with the square root of the flow rate. Subsequent work 38 observed smoke points 
of nonbuoyant flames aboard a parabolic aircraft and used numerical predictions to

show that residence time increases with flame length for nonbuoyant flames without 
coflow. Urban et al. 39 reported smoke points of microgravity flames observed on a 
space shuttle. However, microgravity smoke point measurements are difficult in 
parabolic aircraft owing to g-jitter and in drop facilities owing to limited test times. 
 
1.5. Velocity Field Effects 
By varying the burner diameter, coflow velocity, and fuel dilution, flame shape and 
residence times in the soot formation and soot oxidation regions can be changed. 
Reductions in the burner (fuel jet exit) diameter increase the mean fuel jet velocity, 
reducing overall flame residence time, assuming that flame length only depends on 
the mass flow rate of fuel. There has not been substantial research into the burner 
diameter effect on smoke points. The work of Kent and Wagner 25 showed that 
reducing burner diameter (increasing fuel jet velocity) shifts the centerline soot-
volume-fraction profile downstream, without modifying peak values. Therefore it 
should be expected that the smoke point luminous flame length

volume-fraction profile downstream, without modifying peak values. Therefore it 
should be expected that the smoke point luminous flame length should increase from 
the soot profile shifting downstream, directly lengthening the flame or reducing the 
region of the flame where soot formation is possible. Increasing fuel dilution, in 
addition to modifying soot propensity by volumetric and thermal effects, increases the 
fuel jet velocity at a particular mass flow rate of hydrocarbon fuel. 
 
An increase in coflow velocity will generally decrease entrainment towards the flame 
axis. The coflow velocity can modify the residence time by countering flow 
deceleration in nonbuoyant flames, and accelerating flow in both nonbuoyant and

velocity fields modified by these previously mentioned factors as their flow is not 
subject to buoyancy related acceleration, which can tend to dominate the flow field.16 
 
Schalla and McDonald 34 were the first to investigate the effects of coflow velocity on 
the smoke point of laminar diffusion flames. Their work showed that increasing 
coflow velocity increased the fuel mass flow rate at the smoke point up to a point, 
after which the effect ceases. A modified plot of their results is shown in Figure 1.1. 
Berry-Yelverton and Roberts 40 showed that the smoke point of ethylene increased 
with decreasing initial fuel to air velocity ratio, and therefore with increasing coflow 
velocity, as shown in Figure 1.2. These tests were over a range of fuel/air velocity 
ratios, 0.6 - 1.4. The results of Schalla and McDonald were also over an initial fuel to
