Smoke Point In Coflow Experiment 
“SPICE” 
Microgravity Science Glovebox 
Increment 19-20 (30 Day Report) 
Investigators: David Urban NASA GRC, Peter Sunderland: Univ. Maryland 
Project Scientist: Zengguang Yuan, National Center for Space Exploration Research 
Project Manager: Robert Hawersaat NASA GRC 
 
I. Introduction 
 
A. Hypothesis 
The hypothesis of the SPICE investi gation is that smoke point behavior 
will be observed for co-flowing flames and that it will show 
dependence on nozzle diameter and coflow velocity. 
 
B. Objectives of Investigation 
The objective of the SPICE experiment is to find the laminar smoke-point 
properties of nonbuoyant jet diffusion flames (i.e., the properties of the 
largest laminar jet diffusion flames that do not emit soot) for several fuels 
under different nozzle diameter/ co-flow velocity configurations. 
Luminous flame shape measurements would also be made to verify 
models of the flame shapes under co-flow conditions. 
 
C. Previous Mission Experience 
 N/A 
 
D. Background/History of Project (Optional) 
 The SPICE experiment was an outgrow

passages.title: SPICE 30-DayPostFlightReport
passages.text:
models of the flame shapes under co-flow conditions. 
 
C. Previous Mission Experience 
 N/A 
 
D. Background/History of Project (Optional) 
 The SPICE experiment was an outgrow th of the Laminar Soot Processes 
Experiment (LSP) which flew on STS 83, 94, and 107. SPICE utilized the 
design heritage and modified the hardware from the Enclosed Laminar Flames 
Experiment (ELF) which flew in the Middeck Glovebox on STS 87. 
 
II. Methods/Research Operations 
 
A. Discussion of Method/Protocol 
 Most tests were conducted by setting the coflow velo city, igniting the flame, 
and adjusting the fuel flow rate. Appr oximate smoke points were identified in 
the video by the flight crew and simultaneously by the ground support crew in 
Cleveland. Typical burn times were 60 s, and after each two such burns the 
MSG contents were flushed with ISS cabin air. After the tests the video 
record was analyzed to identify sm oke point conditions. The associated 
coflow and fuel flow rates were obtain ed from digital data recorded in the 
video. The smoke point lengths, LSP, we re obtained from the vid

passages.title: SPICE 30-DayPostFlightReport
passages.text:
oke point conditions. The associated 
coflow and fuel flow rates were obtain ed from digital data recorded in the 
video. The smoke point lengths, LSP, we re obtained from the video record 
and are the measured distance from the burner tip to the tip of the luminous 
flame on the flame axis.

passages.title: SPICE 30-DayPostFlightReport
passages.text:
III. Results 
 
A. List of Preflight, In-flight, Postflight Anomalies 
 SPICE operated very successfully with the only significant anomaly being the 
accumulation of soot in the outlet screen which changed the flow behavior in 
the duct. This was corrected by a crew member using the vacuum to clean the 
outlet screen on June 15. 
B. Completeness/Quality of Data 
During Increment 18 SPICE conducted 108 test points completing its nominal 
test matrix. During Increments 19/20 SPICE conducted 155 additional test 
points the provided improved resolution of the smoke points and allowed us to 
explore further limits in the parameter space. 
C. Status of Data Analysis: The data from the down linked video have been analyzed 
for flame length and smoke point flow rate. These have resulted in a meeting apper 
and a draft journal paper. More work will be conducted with analysis of the digital 
luminance data from the Nikon. 
 
D. Preliminary Research Findings: 
 See attached paper below

2009 Fall Technical Meeting 
Organized by the Eastern States Section of the Combustion Institute 
and Hosted by the University of Maryland College Park 
October 18-21, 2009 
Laminar Smoke Points of 
Microgravity Coflow Diffusion Flames 
K.T. Dotsona, P.B. Sunderlanda, Z.–G. Yuanb, D.L. Urbanc 
aDepartment of Fire Protection Engineering, University of Maryland, College Park, MD, USA 
bNational Center for Space Exploration Research, Cleveland, OH, USA 
cNASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH, USA 
 
Laminar smoke points were measured in nonbuoyant laminar jet diffusion flames in air coflow aboard the 
International Space Station as part of the Smoke Points in Coflow Experiment (SPICE). Smoke points were found 
for ethylene, propane, propylene, and mixtures of 50 and 75% propylene by volume in nitrogen. Burner diameters 
were 0.41, 0.76 and 1.6 mm and coflow velocities varied from 5.4 – 65 cm/s. These flames afford good control over 
residence time via variations in dilution, burner diameter , and coflow velocity. Increasing coflow velocity decreases 
luminous flame lengths, but m

passages.title: SPICE 30-DayPostFlightReport
passages.text:
ames afford good control over 
residence time via variations in dilution, burner diameter , and coflow velocity. Increasing coflow velocity decreases 
luminous flame lengths, but moves smoke points to higher fuel flow rates and longer luminous flame lengths. 
Smaller burners have longer smoke points for coflowing flames. These trends can be explained qualitatively by 
considering total residence time effects. The luminous flame lengths generally correlate with fuel mass flow rate 
divided by stoichiometric mixture fraction, although they increase slightly as air velocity decreases. 
1. Introduction 
Soot formation is an important unresolved problem in combustion science. Soot is estimated to 
be responsible for up to 50,000 prem ature deaths in the U.S. [1] a nd is believed to contribute to 
climate change and glacial melting [2]. Radiation from soot in flames allows reading by candle-
light but also contributes to he at loads in engines and the spread of unwanted fires. Smoking 
flames emit carbon monoxide, which is the major cause of death in fires [3]. 
The smoke point is the cond

passages.title: SPICE 30-DayPostFlightReport
passages.text:
butes to he at loads in engines and the spread of unwanted fires. Smoking 
flames emit carbon monoxide, which is the major cause of death in fires [3]. 
The smoke point is the condition (or length) where a flame begi ns to emit soot. Smoke points 
indicate the sooting propensity of a fuel in diffusion flames. In normal gravity, laminar smoke 
points have been measured for many gaseous a nd condensed fuels [4–9]. Laminar smoke points 
have been found to correl ate with soot volume frac tions [10] and radiative loss factions [11] of 
turbulent diffusion flames. Yang et al. [12] found that gas turbine soot em issions correlate very 
well with a threshold sooting i ndex (TSI) based on fuel molecula r weight divided by the laminar 
smoke point. Smoke points have been shown to co rrelate with the smoke release from turbulent 
buoyant flames [13] and have been applied to developing general soot models for computational 
combustion simulations [14] and heat release measurements [15]. 
In a 1988 paper [16], Glassman predicted that smoke points would not occur in nonbuoyant gas-
jet flames. He

passages.title: SPICE 30-DayPostFlightReport
passages.text:
ional 
combustion simulations [14] and heat release measurements [15]. 
In a 1988 paper [16], Glassman predicted that smoke points would not occur in nonbuoyant gas-
jet flames. He based this on the assumption that residence time scales with the square root of fuel 
flow rate in normal gravity but is independent of flow rate in microgravity flames. Subsequent 
work [17] observed smoke points of nonbuoyant fl ames aboard a parabolic aircraft and used 
numerical predictions to show that residence time increases with flame length for nonbuoyant 
flames without co-flow. Urban et al. [18] reported smoke points of microgravity flames observed 
on a space shuttle. Microgravity smoke point meas urements are difficult in parabolic aircraft

passages.title: SPICE 30-DayPostFlightReport
passages.text:
2 
owing to g-jitter and in drop facilities owing to limited test times. 
Attributing smoke point behavior to total resi dence time helps with qualitative explanations of 
smoke point behavior but to date has not yielded successful quant itative correlations [8]. This 
may be because smoke points arise from a comp etition between the times available for soot 
formation and soot oxidation. De lichatsios and co-workers suggest ed that smoke point length is 
proportional to soot formation time [19–20]. Quantitative correlations may also be possible from 
an examination of radiative losses, which have been observed to be 20 – 30% for normal-gravity 
smoke point flames and to increase with adiabatic flame temperature [5]. 
Soot is transported in flames by convection and thermophoresis. By varying the burner diameter, 
coflow velocity, and fuel dilution, flame shape and residence times in the soot formation and 
soot oxidation regions can be changed. A decrease in coflow velocity will generally increase 
entrainment of flow towards the flame axis. 
Kent and Wagner [21] found that smoke bur

passages.title: SPICE 30-DayPostFlightReport
passages.text:
soot oxidation regions can be changed. A decrease in coflow velocity will generally increase 
entrainment of flow towards the flame axis. 
Kent and Wagner [21] found that smoke burn out in the oxidat ive region of the flame ceases 
when the tip of a buoyant diffusion flame cools to approximately 1300 K. Urban et al. [22] found 
that the tip of a nonbuoyant (microgravity) fl ame reaches 1000 K at its smoke point. In buoyant 
flames this decrease in temperature is attr ibuted primarily to he at conduction, while in 
nonbuoyant flames it is attributed largely to ra diative quenching [23]. The radiative quenching 
effect causes a visible tip openi ng in nonbuoyant smoke points of flames of relatively long 
residence time [22]. 
A recent 2.5 s drop tower study by Jeon et al. [24] found that for small coflow velocities the soot 
volume fraction increases with coflow velocit y. This was attributed to an increase in 
temperature. Lin and Faeth [7,25] studied the effects of coflow velocity on weakly-buoyant 
flames near the smoke point. They observed flam es in normal gravity, but at low pres

passages.title: SPICE 30-DayPostFlightReport
passages.text:
n 
temperature. Lin and Faeth [7,25] studied the effects of coflow velocity on weakly-buoyant 
flames near the smoke point. They observed flam es in normal gravity, but at low pressures to 
reduce the effects of gravity. They found that increasing the coflow velocity reduced soot 
volume fractions and increased the smoke point le ngth. This was attributed to decreased flame 
residence time and modified soot pathlines. Refs. [7 and 24] both showed that luminous flame 
lengths decrease with increasi ng coflow velocity. Their bur ner diameters, 7 and 10 mm, 
respectively, were much larger than those considered here. 
Faeth and co-workers [25–27] applied the fl ame shape analyses of Spalding [28] and 
Mahalingam et al. [29] to nonbuoyant gas-jet flames to obtain

Schmidt number and viscosity, defined in this fashion, do not vary substantially for the flames in

Thus motivated, the objectives of this study are: 
1. to measure nonbuoyant smoke points of propane, ethylene, propylene, and 
propylene/nitrogen mixtures, 
2. to identify the effects of coflow velocity and burner diameter on the smoke points, and 
3. to correlate the luminous flame lengths. 
2. Experimental 
The Smoke Points in Coflow Experiment (SPI CE) module was brought to the International 
Space Station (ISS) in 2008. It was operated in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) by 
various crew members in 2009. Smoke points were at tempted for all fuels for fuel jet diameters 
of 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 mm. The conditions for which smoke points were found are summarized in 
Table 1. In some cases (e.g., te sts involving ethylene) the fuel supply was depleted before 
desired smoke points could be found, as the supply was limited to two 75 cc bottles of each fuel 
at gage pressures of 760 – 1440 kPa, depending on the fuel. 
 The SPICE module contains a rectangular duct th at has an approximately 76

passages.title: SPICE 30-DayPostFlightReport
passages.text:
limited to two 75 cc bottles of each fuel 
at gage pressures of 760 – 1440 kPa, depending on the fuel. 
 The SPICE module contains a rectangular duct th at has an approximately 76 mm square cross 
section with rounded corners. A DC fan supplie s coflowing air from the glovebox contents. The 
air passes through a honeycomb and screen to reduce swirl and then enters the duct. The air and 
combustion products leave the duct through a pe rforated copper plate followed by a copper 
screen. The screen is 50 mm upstream of th e burner discharge and the plate is 120 mm 
downstream. Fan voltage is varied to control the coflow velocity, which is measured with a hot-
wire anemometer between the inlet honeycomb a nd screen. This anemometer was calibrated in 
normal gravity using a hot-wire anemometer 36 mm downstream of the duct entrance. Fuel flow 
rate was adjusted manually and controlled with a mass flow meter. The flames were ignited with 
a hot-wire ignitor. Video was recorded with an analog color video camera and downlinked in real 
time. Still images were recorded with a 12 bit Nikon™ D1

passages.title: SPICE 30-DayPostFlightReport
passages.text:
flames were ignited with 
a hot-wire ignitor. Video was recorded with an analog color video camera and downlinked in real 
time. Still images were recorded with a 12 bit Nikon™ D100 single-lens reflex color digital still 
camera (with 3008 × 2000 pixels) with a 60 mm lens. 
Most of the tests were conducted by setting the coflow velocity, igniting the flame, and adjusting 
the fuel flow rate. Approximate smoke points were identified in the video by the flight crew and 
simultaneously by the ground support crew in Cleveland. Typical burn times were 60 s, and after 
each two such burns the MSG contents were flushed with ISS cabin air. 
After the tests the video record was analyzed to identify smoke point conditions. The associated 
coflow and fuel flow rates were obtained from digital data r ecorded in the video. The smoke 
point lengths, LSP, were obtained from the vi deo record and are the measured distance from the 
burner tip to the tip of the luminous flame on the flame axis. The luminous flame tips were not 
sharply defined in most images, but rather involved a transition from br

passages.title: SPICE 30-DayPostFlightReport
passages.text:
from the 
burner tip to the tip of the luminous flame on the flame axis. The luminous flame tips were not 
sharply defined in most images, but rather involved a transition from bright yellow to black 
across an axial distance of 2 – 5 mm. Flame hei ght was thus measured to the point where the 
centerline grayscale intensity changed most rapidly between these yellow and black regions. This 
helped reduce the sensitivity of measured flame height to camera exposure settings. 
Smoke points were obtained for five fuels, as summarized in Table 1. Smoke points were

passages.title: SPICE 30-DayPostFlightReport
passages.text:
4 
attempted with methane, but could not be obtained before the flames impinged on the plate at the 
end of the duct. Also shown in Table 1 are the ranges of various parameters for which 
microgravity smoke points were observed. 
3. Results and Discussion 
Some smoke points, propane and ethylene in part icular, were identified by the onset of gradual 
(rather than sharp) dimming and reddening of the luminous flame tip in the downstream 
direction. Rounding of the tip al so was associated with th e smoke point. For conditions 
sufficiently above the smoke point, quenched soot could be seen leaving the flame. The brightest 
flames did not always display significant redden ing or darkening near their tips, except well 
above the smoke point. This occurred for the pu re propylene and propylene mixtures, and the 
smoke point was identified by the rapid transition to an open-tipped, soot emitting flame. 
The flames generally reached steady conditions within 5 s of ignition or a change in flow rate of 
fuel or air. Flames of propylene and propylene mixtures were generally more luminous than

passages.title: SPICE 30-DayPostFlightReport
passages.text:
es generally reached steady conditions within 5 s of ignition or a change in flow rate of 
fuel or air. Flames of propylene and propylene mixtures were generally more luminous than 
those of methane, ethylene, and propane, attribut ed to their higher propensity to form soot. The 
smoke point transition was more abrupt in th e propylene-based fuels than for propane or 
ethylene. Periodic flame motion was observed in some flames, especially those with high coflow, 
long length, and low fuel velocity, and is attributed to non-uniform coflow. This effect was small 
and did not prevent clear measurement of flame length. 
Figure 1 shows images for representative flames near their smoke points. Two sequences are 
shown, and in both the smoke point occurs betw een the third and fourth flames. In the top 
sequence, coflow velocity decreases from left to right at constant fuel flow rate. This increases 
luminous flame length and reduces the smoke poi nt leading to soot emission. The luminous 
length decreases in the fourth image owing to incomplete combustion. In the bottom sequence 
fuel flow

passages.text:
e length and reduces the smoke poi nt leading to soot emission. The luminous 
length decreases in the fourth image owing to incomplete combustion. In the bottom sequence 
fuel flow rate is increased at constant coflow velocity, increasing flame length as expected. As 
seen in Fig. 1, luminous length is more sensitive to changes in fuel flow rate than to changes in 
coflow velocity.

Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) 
Abstract 
The laminar smoke point is the condition (and the luminous flame length) where a flame begins 
to emit soot. Smoke points indicate the sooting propensity of a fuel in diffusion flames. In normal 
gravity, laminar smoke points have been measured for many gaseous and condensed fuels. 
Laminar smoke points have been found to correlate with soot volume fractions and radiative loss 
fractions of turbulent diffusion flames. SPICE project measured laminar smoke points in non)
buoyant laminar jet diffusion flames in co)flowing air aboard the International Space Station. 
Fifty)two smoke points were found for ethylene, propane, propylene, and propylene/nitrogen 
mixtures. Burner diameters were 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 mm and co)flow velocities varied from 5.4 – 
65 cm/s. These flames afford extensive control over residence time via variations in dilution, 
burner diameter, and co)flow velocity. Increasing co)flow velocity decreases luminous flame 
lengths, but moves smoke points to higher fuel flow rates and longer luminous flame lengths.

passages.title: SPICE FinalReport
passages.text:
diameter, and co)flow velocity. Increasing co)flow velocity decreases luminous flame 
lengths, but moves smoke points to higher fuel flow rates and longer luminous flame lengths. 
Smaller burners have longer smoke points for co)flowing flames. These trends can be explained 
qualitatively by considering total residence time effects. The luminous flame lengths generally 
correlate with fuel mass flow rate divided by stoichiometric mixture fraction, although they 
increase slightly as air velocity decreases. The measured smoke point lengths were found to 
correlate with burner diameter to the –0.91 power times coflow velocity to the 0.41 power. The 
measurements allow estimates of pseudo threshold soot indices (TSI) for microgravity diffusion 
flames, indicating an unusually high sooting propensity for propane in microgravity. A model of 
residence times in coflowing flames is developed, and although residence time helps explain 
many of the observations, it does not correlate the measured smoke points. The measurements 
yielded estimates of sooting propensities of the present fuels in

INTRODUCTION 
 
SPICE project, from it was rewarded in 1997 to it was conducted onboard ISS in 2009, covered 
more than a decade time span. During these years, the project experienced a few cycles of active and 
inactive status. A brief project history is given below. SPICE project was awarded on December 3, 
1997 by the Microgravity Science and Application Division of NASA Headquarters to Professor 
Gerard M. Faeth of the University of Michigan for his proposal titled as Laminar Smoke Point 
Properties of Nonbuoyant Round-Jet Diffusion Flames in response to NASA’s 1996 Solicitation for 
Glovebox Investigations issued in late 1996. The original proposal of Professor Faeth was meant to 
be a supplement to the Laminar Soot Processes Experiment which was a combustion project under 
NASA Grant No. NAG3-1245, conducted onboard STS-73 and STS-94 in 1997. In the awarding 
letter, the experiment was planned to be carried out onboard STS-107, for which the launch date was 
then scheduled in May 2000. From December 1997 to the end of 1999 was the first phase of the 
project. In this per

then scheduled in May 2000. From December 1997 to the end of 1999 was the first phase of the 
project. In this period, the experiment was planned to be conducted in the Middle Deck Glove Box 
of a Space Shuttle and the SPICE hardware was fabricated and assembled in GRC. Various project 
reviews necessary for the flight project, were completed. In addition, significant efforts on science

March 2002, the project was inactive. The second phase of the project was from March 2002 to 
January 2005. In this period, SPICE was a part of MRDOC contract to ZIN Inc., for a potential UF-1 
Flight. Since the target facility of SPICE was switched from Space Shuttle’s Middle Deck Glove 
Box to the ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG), ZIN’s major effort was to retro-fit hardware 
for use with MSG in International Space Station (ISS), whi

Soot formation in hydrocarbon-fueled flames is an important unresolved problem in combustion 
science. Soot i

passages.title: SPICE FinalReport

is the science significance and justification of the SPICE project. 
 
Soot formation in hydrocarbon-fueled flames is an important unresolved problem in combustion 
science. Soot is estimated to be responsible for up to 52,000 premature deaths annually in the U.S. 1 
and is believed to contribute to climate change and glacial melting. 2 Radiation from soot in flames is 
beneficial in many applications but also contributes to unwanted heat loads in engines and the spread 
of fires. Carbon monoxide emitted by smoking flames is the major cause of death in fires. 3 
Knowledge of Soot formation is needed for developing computational combustion.

passages.title: SPICE FinalReport
passages.text:
2 
 
The differences between soot processes in buoyant and nonbuoyant laminar jet diffusion flames can 
be seen by comparing their soot production regions as plotted in Fig. 1. Soot formation in diffusion 
flames generally is limited to fuel-equivalence ratios, φ, in the range 1-2, which are marked on the 
plots. Unlike gases, which both convect and diffuse, soot mainly convects with the flow velocity so 
that it moves along the streamline. For buoyant flames, the dividing streamline generally is inside 
the soot formation region so that most of the soot initially forms near the flame sheet, where φ, =1, 
and then moves radially inward toward cooler regions having higher fuel concentrations. The soot 
formation process for nonbuoyant flames is completely different: most of the soot initially forms 
near the cool core of the flame, where φ is close to 2, and is drawn directly toward the flame sheet. 
Results from an MSL-1 combustion project, the Laminar Soot Processes (LSP), revealed that the 
smoke height phenomenon in microgravity can be substantially different form that seen in nor

passages.title: SPICE FinalReport
passages.text:
from an MSL-1 combustion project, the Laminar Soot Processes (LSP), revealed that the 
smoke height phenomenon in microgravity can be substantially different form that seen in normal 
gravity. The removal of buoyancy induced acceleration can cause the smoke point phenomenon to 
be dominated by radiative heat losses for conditions of low overall flame velocity. Under these 
conditions the flame extinguishes at the flame tip allowing soot to be emitted. In spite of this effect, 
it is still possible to have flames that either emit soot along all stream lines or do not emit soot 
anywhere, for conditions where radiation losses do not dominate. 
 
 
 
Figure 1. Soot path lines through buoyant and non-buoyant flames 
 
The information of smoke-point properties and flame shapes is needed to improve our understanding 
of heat and mass transfer mechanisms for different flame conditions. Unfortunately, while the 
laminar smoke-point properties of buoyant jet diffusion flames at normal gravity are well known, 
corresponding information for nonbuoyant flames is limited and questionable. Thus t

passages.title: SPICE FinalReport
passages.text:
aminar smoke-point properties of buoyant jet diffusion flames at normal gravity are well known, 
corresponding information for nonbuoyant flames is limited and questionable. Thus the insights of 
soot generation and oxidation processes under microgravity conditions are critical to devise better 
fire safety strategy in spacecraft needed for long term space travels and other space exploration 
activities. In addition, the improved understanding of soot processes in laminar flames will help us, 
by analogy, to gain better understanding of soot processes in practical turbulent flames. 
 
 
The objectives of the SPICE experiments is to find the laminar smoke-point properties of non-
buoyant jet diffusion flames for several fuels under different nozzle diameter/co-flow velocity 
configurations. Luminous flame shape measurements would also be made to verify models of the

passages.title: SPICE FinalReport
passages.text:
3 
 
flame shapes under co-flow conditions. In particular, the experiments are planned to be conducted 
under the following conditions: six types of fuels: methane, ethylene, propane, propylene, 75% 
propylene mixed with 25% nitrogen in moles, and 50% propylene mixed with 50% nitrogen in moles; 
three nozzles: 0.4, 0.8 and 1.6 mm ID and two air velocities: 100% and 50% of the maximum air 
flow velocity (near 50cm/s). The operation procedures are as such that the air velocity is set first, 
then start the fuel flow and ignite the flame. Fuel flow rate is adjusted until the smoke point is 
reached. Thus, for each combination of a fuel and a nozzle size, two smoke point fuel flow rates are 
obtained. One is under 100% air velocity and the other is under 50% air velocity. Then in the case of 
50% air velocity, the fuel flow rate is reduced to 50% of the smoke point fuel flow rate to get a flame 
length with that fuel flow rate.

The SPICE project utilized and modified an apparatus constructed for a previous project, Enclosed

passages.title: NNX17AF08A FinalReport
passages.text:
1 Executive Summary
This work examines how microgravity conditions on spacecraft change the development of smoke
aerosol relative to smoke on Earth. We perform simulations of particle formation and growth with
the goal of capturing smoke dynamics similar to those realized in experiments performed aboard the
International Space Station. The simulations provide detailed information about ﬂuid/thermal/particle
interactions that cannot be acquired experimentally on orbit. A surrogate material, dibutyl pthalate, is
expelled from a hot surface in a rectangular chamber while ambient air is blown through the domain,
convecting the developing smoke downstream. The study considers two ﬂow rates, two geometric con-
ﬁgurations, and the isolated effects of gravitational particle settling and thermophoresis. In Earth gravity,
buoyancy produces asymmetries in all ﬁelds of interest and ampliﬁes vapor-to-particle conversion near
room temperature surfaces at the upper boundary of the simulation domain. Gravitational settling re-
moves large particles from the aerosol, limiting the maximum particle siz

passages.title: NNX17AF08A FinalReport
passages.text:
near
room temperature surfaces at the upper boundary of the simulation domain. Gravitational settling re-
moves large particles from the aerosol, limiting the maximum particle size to ∼ 40 µm and the mode
particle size to ∼ 5 µm. Without buoyancy or settling, the microgravity smoke plume is spatially symmet-
ric and contains very large particles (> 40 µm). A bimodal particle size distribution results in microgravity
when prominent recirculation occurs behind the hot vapor source. The distribution is comprised of large
particles (> 20 µm) associated with long residency time, vapor rich, high temperature recirculation, and
smaller particles (< 10 µm) that originate farther downstream of the hot vapor source. A distinct large
particle mode does not appear in microgravity ﬂows that do not have prominent high temperature re-
circulation, although the aerosol still contains large particles. Without recirculation, the mode particle
diameter in microgravity is ∼ 10 µm, or approximately twice that of terrestrial smoke. Results show that
future experiments should carefully consider and quanti

passages.title: NNX17AF08A FinalReport
passages.text:
, the mode particle
diameter in microgravity is ∼ 10 µm, or approximately twice that of terrestrial smoke. Results show that
future experiments should carefully consider and quantify surface interactions and the presence of hot,
recirculating vapor, in order to control geometry-dominated features of the particle size distribution.
A manuscript based on this work will be submitted to the journal Aerosol Science & Technology. The
ﬁnal document, when accepted, will be provided to NASA.

passages.title: NNX17AF08A FinalReport
passages.text:
2 Introduction
Gravity affects the evolution of aerosols by introducing buoyancy and particle settling. Buoyant convec-
tion modiﬁes the time-temperature history of the aerosol, as well as the spatial distribution of particles,
condensing vapor, and thermal energy. Gravity also causes the settling of large particles out of the
aerosol, provided the chemistry and vapor concentrations allow for the generation of large particles
with appreciable settling velocities. These factors combine to increase particle residency times in high
temperature, vapor rich regions in microgravity systems relative to terrestrial or Earth gravity systems
(Urban et al., 1998, 2005). As a result, smoke particles produced in microgravity tend to be larger than
those produced on Earth (Ku et al., 1995, Urban et al., 1998). Measurements suggest microgravity
smoke particles to be 2 − 8 times larger than terrestrial smoke particles (Urban et al., 2005). Moreover,
large particles (not only smoke particles) persist in microgravity, with mass concentrations of particles
with diameter > 100 µm measured at ten-times t

passages.title: NNX17AF08A FinalReport
passages.text:
an et al., 2005). Moreover,
large particles (not only smoke particles) persist in microgravity, with mass concentrations of particles
with diameter > 100 µm measured at ten-times that of a nominal terrestrial environment (Liu et al.,
1991). Total particulate mass concentrations are also more than ﬁve times greater in microgravity (Liu
et al., 1991). Understanding gravitational effects is of practical interest because it assists in the design
of mission-critical smoke detection systems for use in microgravity environments, including the Interna-
tional Space Station (Mulholland et al., 2015); systems developed and calibrated for terrestrial use may
not perform correctly in microgravity because of inappropriate particle size sensitivities (Urban et al.,
2005).
The present work uses numerical simulation to explore the inﬂuence of gravity on pyrolysis smoke
growth from a fundamental perspective. We simulate the formation and growth of dibutyl-phthalate
(DBP) particles in Earth gravity and microgravity environments. We utilize direct numerical simulation
via a Navier-Stokes nodal approach

passages.title: NNX17AF08A FinalReport
passages.text:
formation and growth of dibutyl-phthalate
(DBP) particles in Earth gravity and microgravity environments. We utilize direct numerical simulation
via a Navier-Stokes nodal approach. The smoke originates from pyrolysis vapor expelled from a heated
sample in a geometry similar to that considered in the SAME experiments (Mulholland et al., 2015). The
intention of this effort is to quantify the differences between microgravity and Earth gravity smoke, and
to identify the ﬂuid dynamic mechanisms that cause the differences. This study considers two cross-
ﬂow velocities of sufﬁciently low speed that buoyancy cannot be neglected in the presence of gravity.
Simulations are presented to assess the dependence of particle size distributions on thermophoresis,
particle settling, and ﬂow geometry. The paper is organized as follows: we introduce the simulation and
modeling methodology, followed by a description of the ﬂow geometry and the parameter space under
consideration; we then examine differences in the wake geometry attributable to buoyancy for the lower
of two ﬂow speeds; next, we present

passages.title: NNX17AF08A FinalReport
passages.text:
w geometry and the parameter space under
consideration; we then examine differences in the wake geometry attributable to buoyancy for the lower
of two ﬂow speeds; next, we present and discuss instantaneous scalar ﬁelds as a means to describe
particle accumulation and growth in the buoyant and non-buoyant wakes that form downstream of the
hot vapor source; after developing an understanding of how the particle ﬁelds interact with the ﬂuid
dynamics for the low speed cases, we consider the effects of thermophoresis, particle settling, ﬂow
geometry, and the higher ﬂow speed; we conclude with a discussion of the results, summarize ﬁndings
relevant to future experimentation, and outline directions for future work.

4 Results
4.1 FLOW CONFIGURATION
We simulate the formation and growth of DBP particles in air ﬂowing over a heated sample that expels
DBP vapor. The simulation mimics the smoldering or pre-conﬂagration stage of a ﬁre studied in experi-
ments performed aboard the ISS (Mulholland et al., 2015). A schematic of the computational domain is
shown in Fig. 1. Room temperature air enters a long chamber and ﬂows over a heated rectangular sam-
ple. Vapor released from the sample nucleates into particles that grow and are subsequently collected
downstream for analysis. The ﬂow is laminar and steady, allowing the two-dimensional representation
to present physical characteristics largely representative of the SAME experiments (Mulholland et al.,
2015). DBP is used as the surrogate material because its properties are known and its use in modeling
is well-established (unlike the materials used in the SAME experiments).
4.2 PHYSICAL CONDITIONS
Constant ﬂuid properties for air and DBP are provided in Table 1, and variable DBP properties are
provided in Table 2. The enhancement factor required for the

PHYSICAL CONDITIONS
Constant ﬂuid properties for air and DBP are provided in Table 1, and variable DBP properties are
provided in Table 2. The enhancement factor required for the nucleation expression, Eqn. (20), is
deﬁned for DBP as cnuc = 3.2 × 10−4 (Nguyen et al., 1987, Pyyk¨onen and Jokiniemi, 2000).
The thickness of the heated DBP source serves as the reference length scale, Lo = 0.0044 m (illustrated
in Fig. 1), which is representative of the length scale in the SAME experiments (Mulholland et al.,
2015). The air enters from the left with velocity Uo and temperature To = 300 K. We consider two
inlet velocities: Uo = 0.08 m/s, the velocity considered in the SAME experiments, and a slightly faster
ﬂow of Uo = 0.10 m/s. The upper and lower boundaries are impermeable, no-slip, iso-thermal surfaces
(Twall = To). The heated rectangle is also no-slip, has a ﬁxed temperature of Ts = 473.2 K, and releases
DBP vapor at a constant mass ﬂux of q′′ = 8.4 × 10−5 kg/m2 · s. The mass ﬂux has been selected to be
representative of the mass loss data presented by Mulholland et al. (2015). Zero-d

representative of the mass loss data presented by Mulholland et al. (2015). Zero-derivative conditions
are imposed for all species and particle ﬁelds at the inlet and outlet. The gravitational acceleration is
considered at terrestrial (go = 9.81 m/s2) and microgravity (go = 0 m/s2) conditions.
The inlet velocities and the gravitational accelerations considered represent four cases with varying
Reynolds and Froude numbers. A summary of the simulations performed at the two ﬂow speeds and

gravity” conditions, while 1 and 2 identify the Uo = 0.08 m/s and Uo = 0.1 m/s conditions, respectively.
Case 1MG is therefore deﬁned to have an inlet velocity of Uo = 0.08 m/s and go = 0 m/s2, corre-
sponding to a Reynolds number Re = 22.3 and a Froude number Fr = ∞. In addition to the four base
cases listed in Table 3, we examine the aerosol development sensitivity to: (1) particle settling, (2) ther

3, are constructed by modifying the setup of Case 1MG and/or Case 1EG. Case 1EG-NS (where NS

4.4 PHYSICAL ASSUMPTIONS
All assumptions utilized in this work are listed below.
• From the perspective of thermal conductivity and viscosity, the condensing vapor phase is con-
sidered sufﬁciently dilute such that µ and k are computed for air as a function of temperature and
density (Kadoya et al., 1985). Both the air and the condensing vapor are considered calorically
perfect gases with constant properties deﬁned in Table 1.
• The Mach number M is only important for ﬂows with M & 0.3. Although the physics are insen-
sitive to variation in Mach number when the Mach number is small, the ratio of sound speed to
convective speed imposes a large computational burden. The computational challenge is often
remedied with a Boussinesq app

passages.title: NNX17AF08A FinalReport
passages.text:
hen the Mach number is small, the ratio of sound speed to
convective speed imposes a large computational burden. The computational challenge is often
remedied with a Boussinesq approximation, but this approach is not valid in the presence of large
density variations. Additionally, an elliptical solve for pressure is computationally intractable for the
number of iterations required to resolve the particle time scales. We instead use a scaled dynamic
pressure as the reference pressure Po = ρo (c1Uo)2, such that P⋆ = ραRαT Po , where c1 is speciﬁed to reduce the effective speed of sound to 8 m/s. The ﬂow ﬁeld was found to be independent of c1
for the values used.
• All particles are assumed to be spherical.
• Condensed phase DBP properties are deﬁned by their continuum values.
• There is no momentum exchange between the particles and the ﬂuid (the air/DBP vapor mixture);
the particle velocity equals the ﬂuid velocity, augmented by the thermophoretic velocity and the
stokes settling velocity. The stokes settling velocity is assumed to apply for all particles in the
domain (including the

passages.title: NNX17AF08A FinalReport
passages.text:
elocity, augmented by the thermophoretic velocity and the
stokes settling velocity. The stokes settling velocity is assumed to apply for all particles in the
domain (including the large particles).
• The ﬂuid and particles are in thermal equilibrium and have the same temperature.
• Particle diffusion coefﬁcients decrease rapidly with diameter. This poses a numerical challenge
due to the lack of a physical mechanism for diffusing numerical errors. For this reason, the mini-
mum diffusion coefﬁcient considered in the particle mass fraction transport equations corresponds
to the ﬁfth particle size node – any node greater than the ﬁfth node is assigned the particle diffu-
sion coefﬁcient of the ﬁfth node.
• The mass ﬂux of DPB from the heated rectangle is spatially uniform and all surfaces have spatially
uniform temperature.
• Particles that impact a solid surface “stick” with 100% efﬁciency, and are removed from the ﬂow.
• The aerosol does not achieve a rigorous steady-state because particle evolution continues (slowly)
in regions of the ﬂow with recirculation, particularly behind the h

passages.title: NNX17AF08A FinalReport
passages.text:
om the ﬂow.
• The aerosol does not achieve a rigorous steady-state because particle evolution continues (slowly)
in regions of the ﬂow with recirculation, particularly behind the hot vapor source. The recirculation
is characterized by high temperatures, long particle residency times, and the continuous intro-
duction of additional vapor. The hydrodynamic and thermal ﬁelds, conversely, become steady
after only a few seconds. Although a rigorous steady-state does not exist, all aerosol features
develop and effectively stabilize shortly after the hydrodynamic ﬁelds. We therefore present all
results at time t = 7 seconds, which is considered to be the effective steady-state. At his time, all
ﬁelds are either steady, or changing at a rate that does not affect the conclusions drawn from the
simulations.

4.5 FLUID FLOW, TEMPERATURE, AND MASS FRACTION
The velocity ﬁeld controls the convection of thermal energy, condensible species vapor, and particles.
Vorticity ω, deﬁned as the curl of the velocity vector
ω = ∇× u, (31)
is positive in regions of the ﬂow where ﬂuid rotates counterclockwise, and is negative in regions where
the ﬂuid rotates clockwise. The sign and magnitude of vorticity therefore identiﬁes the location, orienta-
tion, and intensity of vortices and boundary layers.

Case 1EG. The grey rectangles represent the heated vapor source. Red ﬂuid rotates counterclockwise

channel, the ﬂuid at the walls is brought to rest by the no slip condition, signiﬁed by the large vorticity
gradients in the upper and lower left corners of panels (a) and (b). As the ﬂuid travels downstream
from left to right, boundary layers develop symmetrically on the upper and lower walls due to viscous
diffus

from left to right, boundary layers develop symmetrically on the upper and lower walls due to viscous
diffusion. Further downstream, the heated rectangle reduces the cross-sectional ﬂow area, and the
pressure ﬁeld accelerates the ﬂuid through ﬂow paths above and below the heated vapor source. The

4.6 PARTICLE NUCLEATION, NUMBER DENSITY, AND SIZE
The particle nucleation rate is a function of vapor mass fraction and temperature (and pressure). Figure
5 shows the DBP nucleation rate at time t = 7 seconds for Case 1MG in panel (a) and Case 1EG in
panel (b). Panel (a) shows that nucleation occurs exclusively downstream of the heated vapor source in
Case 1MG, and most rapidly at a rate of ∼ 1012 [ m3 · s ]−1 near the periphery of the recirculating wake.
Nucleation does not occur at a signiﬁcant rate anywhere in the wake. The nucleation rate decreases
quickly after approximately ten dimensionless length units downstream of the heated vapor source.
Panel (b) shows two primary zones of nucleation in Case 1EG: downstream of the upper wake vortex
and in the region downstream and above the upper wake vortex, near the upper surface. Nucleation
occurs at a higher rate, ∼ 1014 [ m3 · s ]−1 , in Case 1EG than in Case 1MG.

(a) and (b), respectively. Panel (a) shows a particle number density of

downstream surface of the heated element, indicated in Fig. 1. The collected number density ¯Qk [ m−3]

ABSTRACT
The primary scientific explorations of this thesis work are to better understand (a) 
microgravity fire-suppression of untested extinguisher, (b) combustion kinetic model 
refinement of renewable fuel butanol (C4H9OH) isomers, and (c) directly induced cool 
flame dynamics of higher n-alkane fuels from an isolated small droplet combustion 
perspective employing computational fluid dynamics with comprehensive chemical 
kinetics. The chronological development of the research direction shifts from a relatively 
small fuel like methanol (CH3OH) to heavier straight paraffinic fuel n-decane (n-C10H22). 
The first installment of the thesis is directed towards answering the feasibility of then-
newly considered fire suppressant xenon (Xe) for microgravity space application by the 
National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA). Methanol was used as model 
fuel to assess the combustion behavior under xenon-rich environment. The 
comprehensive analysis revealed that xenon promotes longer burning time and higher 
flame temperature compared to existing other diluents/extinguish

passages.id: PSI-117::PSI-117_Reports_Dissertation_Combustion Behavior Of Sub-Millimeter Sized Oxygenated And N-Alka.pdf::p7::8
passages.docId: PSI-117::PSI-117_Reports_Dissertation_Combustion Behavior Of Sub-Millimeter Sized Oxygenated And N-Alka.pdf
passages.title: Dissertation Combustion Behavior Of Sub-Millimeter Sized Oxygenated And N-Alka
passages.text:
er xenon-rich environment. The 
comprehensive analysis revealed that xenon promotes longer burning time and higher 
flame temperature compared to existing other diluents/extinguishers and can support hot 
flame with much lesser oxygen content than its counterparts. The exceptionally low 
thermal diffusivity of xenon is identified to be responsible for the significantly higher 
peak gas temperature and prolonged burn time. This detailed analysis clearly debilitates 
the potential of xenon as a next-generation fire-suppressant for microgravity applications 
and helped NASA in safeguard financial investment for International Space Station (ISS) 
experiments using xenon.

vii 
The second installment of the thesis outlines the efforts directed towards 
improving the gas phase kinetic model of butanol isomers based on droplet combustion 
experiments and computations. This is a unique contribution where the traditional gas-
phase experiment/theory-driven kinetic model is further refined in light of critical 
recommendations from the droplet combustion analysis. The comprehensive kinetic 
model of Sarathy et al. (Combust. Flame, 2012) is one of the two widely used model for 
butanol isomers which has been extensively validated against homogeneous gas phase 
experiments. The numerical simulation of the butanol droplet combustion experiments at 
atmospheric conditions predicted the faster burning rate and larger flame diameter using 
the above model. An exhaustive perturbation analysis is carried on chemical, 
thermodynamic and transport parameters influences (while simultaneously isolating their 
cross-influences) to pinpoint the root cause of faster burning tendency of the model. The 
synthesized results from this huge variable-matric perturbation reveale

passages.docId: PSI-117::PSI-117_Reports_Dissertation_Combustion Behavior Of Sub-Millimeter Sized Oxygenated And N-Alka.pdf
passages.title: Dissertation Combustion Behavior Of Sub-Millimeter Sized Oxygenated And N-Alka
passages.text:
isolating their 
cross-influences) to pinpoint the root cause of faster burning tendency of the model. The 
synthesized results from this huge variable-matric perturbation revealed that the isomer-
specific species transport parameters were culpable, and recommendations were made to 
update those Lennard-Jones potential parameters. Once updated, the computational 
predictions significantly improves for the Sarathy et al. model based on the feedback 
from droplet combustion. 
The final segment of the thesis discusses the direct initiation of cool flame 
combustion for submillimeter-sized higher n-alkane droplets (n-heptane and n-decane) 
for possible terrestrial experiments without the necessity of radiative extinction as 
frequently encountered onboard the ISS experiments. It has been found that the 
dimensionality of the droplet (Do = 0.5 mm) statistically reduces the possibility of 
achieving direct cool flame burn for the droplet by simply varying the ignition energy

viii 
initiation. Therefore, it was conceptualized that a combination of a reduced ignition 
source and induction chemistry modulation may hold the possibility of direct initiation of 
cool flame for n-C7H16 and n-C10H22 even in ground-based drop tower experiments. To 
facilitate this idea, we numerically investigate the droplet combustion under selective 
ozone (O3) augmented ambient where O3 serves as an induction chemistry modulator 
through its liberation of atomic O via molecular decomposition. The available atomic O 
then reacts with the surrounding fuel producing OH radical, and eventually water and 
heat. This latter heat input acts as a secondary thermal feedback to the droplet surface 
maintaining steady surface burning rate which then stabilizes the cool flame very near the 
droplet surface. It was found that the fuel physical properties, especially flash point, play 
a decisive role in determining the nature of the initial cool flame dynamics and the ozone 
requirements. Higher flash point fuel (here, n-C10H22) is likely to undergo initial dumped 
cool flame oscillation t

passages.text:
ng the nature of the initial cool flame dynamics and the ozone 
requirements. Higher flash point fuel (here, n-C10H22) is likely to undergo initial dumped 
cool flame oscillation than its lower value counterpart (n-C7H16) and will require higher 
O3 loading under identical ambient. In the near-limit condition, such directly introduced 
cool flame fails to attain a steady burn and enters into a continuously evolving oscillatory 
cool flame. Analyses further indicate that the dynamic interaction of degenerate chain 
branching and chain termination/propagation reaction classes of QOOH (Q=CnH2n) 
species associated with the low-temperature kinetic regimes, and continuous fuel leakage 
across the flame location contribute to the ever-increasing trends of the oscillation 
magnitude.

PREFACE
This thesis reports the combustion behavior of sphero-symmetric small droplets 
for two different classes of fuels (oxygenated alcohols and n-alkanes) under diversified 
ambient conditions with the individual unique objective for each study. The research 
outcomes from this dissertation work were timely published in the leading combustion 
field-specific journals. The author prepared the thesis chapters 3-7 (in consultation with 
the thesis adviser) from those published articles with necessary amendments following 
the guidelines from the graduate school of the University of South Carolina, SC, USA. 
As a consequence, chapter relevant thorough background information from literature is 
provided at the beginning of each chapter. However, an abridged critical review of the 
droplet combustion literature is also included in the 1st chapter to complement the 
rationale of this Ph.D. work. It should be noted that the necessary approval from the

1. Overview 
The Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G) experiment is one of six independent experiments that 
make up the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project for which the tests were 
conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS). 
 
The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) is Prof. Peter B. Sunderland of the Department of Fire 
Protection Engineering at the University of Maryland. The two Co-Investigators (Co-Is) are Profs. Richard 
L. Axelbaum and Forman A. Williams who are respectively from the Washington University of St. Louis and 
the University of California, San Diego (UCSD). 
 
Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NASA Glenn Research Center is the Project Scientist (PS) for ACME 
including CFI-G and the rest of the ACME investigations. In ACME’s preparatory drop testing, etc., Dr. 
Fumiaki Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) served as the Deputy Project Scientist. 
For ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA scienc

passages.title: FinalRpt ACME.CFI-G
passages.text:
drop testing, etc., Dr. 
Fumiaki Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) served as the Deputy Project Scientist. 
For ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team included Drs. Uday G. Hegde and Vedha 
Nayagam who are also with CWRU. 
 
The ISS operations for CFI-G were conducted from March to Oct. 2021 in two sequential rounds of testing. 
The two rounds occurred during Increments 64-65 and 65-66 and respectively featured normal and 
inverse flames. The inverse flame tests were conducted with the chamber filled with a mixture of nitrogen 
and gaseous fuel while an oxygen/nitrogen mixture flowed from the burner. As a result, the inverse 
flames were effectively inside out, e.g., where the soot formed outside rather than inside of the flames. 
Although it was in the second round, the final day of CFI-G testing was carried out in the normal flame 
configuration, with gaseous fuel (with or without nitrogen) flowing into an oxygen/nitrogen atmosphere. 
This was an added test day carried out under conditions in which low-temperature combustion occurred 
during the

or without nitrogen) flowing into an oxygen/nitrogen atmosphere. 
This was an added test day carried out under conditions in which low-temperature combustion occurred 
during the first round of testing. 
 
CFI-G was a late addition to ACME, where the experiment was jointly selected for spaceflight by the 
National Science Foundation (NSF) and the Center for the Advancement of Science in Space (CASIS) rather 
than NASA. The selection was notably announced after the core ACME hardware had launched to the ISS 
and just weeks before ACME’s on-orbit operations began. It is effectively an extension of ACME’s Flame 
Design experiment for which the PI and Co-I are respectively Axelbaum and Sunderland. And it is likewise 
a follow-on to the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI), led by Williams, in which liquid droplets were burned 
rather than gaseous fuel. 
 
Although CFI-G wasn’t selected for spaceflight by NASA, its ISS operations and the development of its 
unique hardware, software, and procedure were carried out by the same teams of personnel as the other

2. Science Overview 
A. Background 
This background is the Project Summary from the experiment’s 2017 proposal in response to a 
solicitation from the NSF/CASIS Collaboration on Combustion and Thermal Transport Processes 
Research on the International Space Station to Benefit Life on Earth. 
 
Overview: 
Cool diffusion flames were discovered in 2012 aboard the ISS. This spawned a rapidly growing 
research field, but only a small number of measurements at limited conditions are available. 
Consequently, cool flame kinetics mechanisms cannot be adequately tested or advanced. This 
could be impeding the development of cleaner and more efficient internal combustion engines. 
 
It is proposed here to observe cool diffusion flames supported by porous spherical burners fed 
with propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. Normal and inverse flames will be considered for a broad 
range of dilution conditions and pressures. The ISS is the ideal platform for observing cool 
diffusion flames because they typically require 20 s to establish and they

passages.title: FinalRpt ACME.CFI-G
passages.text:
r a broad 
range of dilution conditions and pressures. The ISS is the ideal platform for observing cool 
diffusion flames because they typically require 20 s to establish and they could burn indefinitely. 
 
Tests will be performed using the ACME insert in the CIR. Minimal hardware development will be 
required because the spherical porous burners and gas delivery system will be those used by the 
Flame Design flight experiment, while the diagnostics will be those used by the CFI flight 
experiment. 
 
The objectives are to observe diverse cool diffusion flames aboard the ISS, to simulate the tests 
with an advanced CFD model, and to identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that 
accurately models these conditions. 
 
Intellectual Merit: 
Most internal combustion engines are designed using computer models that neglect cool flame 
chemistry, but ignition and flame propagation in engines depend on cool flame chemistry. Cool 
flame chemistry also has a significant impact on fuel octane and cetane numbers, whose 
understanding has large economic consequences. 
 
The proposed exp

passages.title: FinalRpt ACME.CFI-G
passages.text:
ol flame chemistry. Cool 
flame chemistry also has a significant impact on fuel octane and cetane numbers, whose 
understanding has large economic consequences. 
 
The proposed experiments will take advantage of many state-of-the-art diagnostics that are 
already available on the ISS. The flame system to be studied will allow steady spherical cool 
diffusion flames to be observed for the first time. An advanced CFD model will simulate the flames 
and will aid the testing and development of cool flame kinetics models. 
 
Observing cool flames burning as steady spherical diffusion flames will yield valuable insight into 
cool flame chemical kinetics. The measurements proposed cannot be performed in normal gravity 
or in ground-based microgravity facilities. 
 
Broader Impacts: 
The research will be disseminated widely to the combustion research community and to industry. 
It should advance the state-of-the-art in cool flame kinetics mechanisms, which in turn could lead 
to cleaner, more efficient internal combustion engines.

The PI will team with two organizations at UMD - the Women in Engineering Program and the 
Center for Minorities in Science and Engineering - to foster interest in science and engineering 
among female and minority secondary school students. A day-long flame laboratory will be 
developed for secondary school students that will foster their interest in combustion and scientific 
inquiry. 
 
B. Rationale for Microgravity 
This is the ‘Justification for Testing Aboard the ISS’ section (3.1) of the experiment’s 2017 proposal 
in response to a solicitation from the NSF/CASIS Collaboration on Combustion and Thermal 
Transport Processes Research on the International Space Station to Benefit Life on Earth. The 
included equation is formatted differently in this copy. 
 
Previous ground-based microgravity experiments have demonstrated the scientific value of 
spherical, burner-supported diffusion flames. These one-dimensional flames offer a

Previous ground-based microgravity experiments have demonstrated the scientific value of 
spherical, burner-supported diffusion flames. These one-dimensional flames offer a simple, 
fundamental configuration to improve the understanding of diffusion flame behavior and to 
explore such effects as transport, kinetics, soot formation, and radiation, which can be more 
pronounced under microgravity conditions (Atreya et al. 1992; Law et al. 2001; Lecoustre et al. 
2012). 
 
Spherically-symmetric flames are not generally practical in normal gravity. This can be explained 
by considering the Richardson number, which is the ratio of the buoyancy force to the inertial 
force, 
 Ri = g (ΔT L) / (T u2) , (1) 
where g is the acceleration of gravity, T is temperature, L is the characteristic length scale, and u 
is the characteristic velocity. Taking as representative values L = 50 mm, u = 5 cm/s, ΔT = 2000 K, 
and T = 300 K, Ri = 1300 in normal gravity. Ri can be reduced with a judicious choice of fuels and 
inert; Law et al. (2001) have shown that nearly spherical flames can be created

passages.title: FinalRpt ACME.CFI-G
passages.text:
and T = 300 K, Ri = 1300 in normal gravity. Ri can be reduced with a judicious choice of fuels and 
inert; Law et al. (2001) have shown that nearly spherical flames can be created in normal gravity 
using low pressure hydrogen inverse flames. However for typical spherical diffusion flames the 
only way to obtain Ri << 1 is to reduce g by four orders of magnitude. This requires a microgravity 
environment. 
 
Available microgravity drop tower facilities do not offer sufficient time to observe quasi-steady 
spherical diffusion flames, let alone their radiative extinction followed by cool diffusion flames. 
Experiments performed in the 5 s drop facility confirm that typical spherical diffusion flames 
continue growing during 5 s (see Fig. 2). Observations of cool flames in the FLEX, FLEX-2, and CFI 
droplet experiments involved or will involve burn times of up to 60 s. 
 
Analytical work supports these observations of slow flame development. Radial velocities in 
spherical diffusion flames scale with 1 / r2, where r is radius. Thus, at only a few burner diameters 
distance from the sph

passages.title: FinalRpt ACME.CFI-G
passages.text:
ations of slow flame development. Radial velocities in 
spherical diffusion flames scale with 1 / r2, where r is radius. Thus, at only a few burner diameters 
distance from the sphere, diffusion is the dominant transport mechanism. The characteristic 
diffusion time is r2/D, where D is mass diffusivity. For r = 25 mm and D = 20 mm2/s, this diffusion 
time is 30 s. Decreasing the flame size can reduce this time, but will not permit the observation 
of radiative extinction followed by cool diffusion flames. Our analytical and numerical calculations 
indicate that approximately 30 s of jitter-free (less than 10-5 g) microgravity is needed to approach 
quasi-steady state for these flames. The ISS is the only microgravity platform that can provide 
this environment.

C. Science Objectives 
The objectives text presented here is the ‘Hypotheses and Objectives’ section (1.3) of the 
experiment’s 2017 proposal in response to a solicitation from the NSF/CASIS Collaboration on 
Combustion and Thermal Transport Processes Research on the International Space Station to 
Benefit Life on Earth. 
 
The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following for 
the first time, contributing to an improved understanding of cool flame kinetics. 
1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners. 
2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. 
3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures. 
4. Inverse cool diffusion flames. 
5. Cool diffusion flames for which a decrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, 
whereas an increase will cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation 
possible between hot and cool flames. 
 
The research objectives of the proposed work are as follows. 
1. Plan and

passages.title: FinalRpt ACME.CFI-G
passages.text:
ll cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation 
possible between hot and cool flames. 
 
The research objectives of the proposed work are as follows. 
1. Plan and support flight testing on the ISS. 
2. Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, 
and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow 
rate. 
3. Support the flight tests with advanced CFD simulations. 
4. Identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that yields good agreement between 
the CFD predictions and the ISS measurements. 
5. Disseminate the results as widely as possible. 
 
In contrast to objective 2 (and hypothesis 3), it was not feasible with the Combustion Integrated 
Rack (CIR) and ACME chamber insert to conduct tests with n-pentane as proposed (because of its 
low vapor pressure) and testing was instead conducted with ethane as an alternate.

Technical Meeting of the Central States Section of the Combustion Institute, Tulsa, OK, 16–

spaceflight hardware which was mostly launched in 2017. As a result, it does not accurately 
describe the final engineering in some regards. Therefore updates, clarifications, additional 
details, shortcomings, references, etc. have been included in boxed notes like this following the 
original description. As a minor note, the sizes of figures were adjusted in this report, but none 
were cropped. 
 
As previously discussed, the ACME experiments will be conducted within the Combustion 
Integrated Rack (CIR) using a chamber insert, depicted in Figure 2, which was designed to 
accommodate gas delivery to a variety of exchangeable burners. Besides the chamber insert, 
other ACME-unique hardware includes a high-definition color camera and an avionics package, 
which is for data acquisition and control. 
 
 
Figure 2: Design of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) chamber 
insert that will be used in the Combustion Inte

Figure 2: Design of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) chamber 
insert that will be used in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on ISS. 
 
ACME’s chamber insert, which is ~0.4 m in diameter, provides common mounting for a variety of 
burners on the chamber axis (but only one at a time) and includes a retracting resistive igniter. As 
depicted in Figure 3, there will initially be gas-jet burners (with inner diameters ranging from 0.4 
to 3.2 mm), a small coflow burner (where the two concentric tubes have inner diameters of 2.1 
and 25 mm), porous spherical burners (with diameters ranging from 6.35 to 12.7 mm), and two 
flat porous burners for the BRE experiment (with inner diameters of 25 and 50 mm). Most burners 
will be equipped with a surface thermocouple, and each BRE burner will have two heat flux 
transducers. The internal pressure of the porous burners will be measured to allow monitoring 
of the pressure differential across the outlet surface. The igniter will have a crew-exchangeable 
tip and arm (to accomm

of the pressure differential across the outlet surface. The igniter will have a crew-exchangeable 
tip and arm (to accommodate the various burners) and its stepper-motor drive will allow for 
precise positioning.

Figure 3: ACME burner types, including from left to right, gas-jet burners, a co-flow burner, 
porous spherical burners, and flat porous burners for the BRE experiment. 
 
Ultimately, the spherical burners were limited to a single diameter of 6.35 mm, and the fabricated 
gas-jet burners were limited to two sizes with nominal inner diameters of 1.3 and 2.1 mm. 
However, only the larger gas-jet burner was used during the spaceflight tests. The burners are 
addressed in detail in section 3.C. 
 
Unfortunately, the spherical burners have not always yielded spherically symmetric flames, 
presumably as a result of (1) greater burner flow through the joint between the porous sphere and 
supply tube, and (2) heat loss to the support tube (encompassing the supply tube) causing local 
flame quenching. 
 
Two types of igniter tips have been used during ACME testing. Most tests have been conducted 
using a loop igniter tip like those which had been successfully used in the droplet combustion 
experiments which preceded ACME research in

using a loop igniter tip like those which had been successfully used in the droplet combustion 
experiments which preceded ACME research in the CIR. However, some tests were conducted with 
a coil igniter tip, where that included the CFI-G investigation and the second-round testing for both 
the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) and Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-
Flame) experiments, with the exception of the latter’s first day testing. For more information 
about the igniter tips, see section 3.D. 
 
The chamber insert includes three mass flow controllers (visible on the left of Fig. 2) for the 
delivery of fuel, oxidizer or inert (e.g., helium or carbon dioxide), and nitrogen to the burner. The 
maximum fuel flow is 2 slpm (on a nitrogen basis), whereas much higher flows, e.g., 10 slpm (on 
a nitrogen basis), are possible for the oxidizer and nitrogen lines. The crew can exchange the mass 
flow controllers to provide appropriate ranges that maximize the flow accuracy. The gas delivery 
system enables on-orbit dilution of th

flow controllers to provide appropriate ranges that maximize the flow accuracy. The gas delivery 
system enables on-orbit dilution of the fuel or oxidizer (but not both simultaneously), coflow, 
inverse flames (e.g., oxidizer delivery to the center of a coflow burner), and premixed flames, 
although the latter are not planned for any of the current ACME experiments. Gases can also be 
delivered premixed to the space station where that is necessary in some circumstances, such as 
the blending of different fuel gases. CIR’s standard bottle sizes are 1, 2.25, and 3.8 liters but ACME 
will sometimes use smaller bottles as a hazard control to limit the deficient reactant (e.g., fuel) 
that can be released into the combustion chamber. 
 
Thus far, ACME tests were not conducted with carbon dioxide as a diluent. Furthermore, the fuel 
diluted with helium was premixed prior to launch rather than on orbit. Ultimately, oxidizer flows 
of up to 20 slpm (on a nitrogen basis) were possible, while the nitrogen flow was limited to a

bottle fill pressure was instead limited as an additional hazard control. 
 
ACME’s primary flame diagnostics are a suite of imaging systems including five video cameras and 
two illumination systems, of which three cameras are part of the CIR facility and are already in 
use on orbit. All but one of the cameras is mounted outside of the chamber. Collectively, the 
imaging systems will enable color, CH*, and OH* imaging; pyrometry; measurement of the soot 
volume fraction; and operational support. However, it is unlikely that all functions would be 
exercised at any one time as will become apparent in the subsequent discussion. 
 
Color imaging is provided by two cameras: a high-definition digital camera mounted outside of 
the chamber and a standard analog camera mounted on the chamber insert (with a turning 
mirror). Both cameras are part of the ACME hardware that is now in development. The analog 
camera signal will be downlinked in

mirror). Both cameras are part of the ACME hardware that is now in development. The analog 
camera signal will be downlinked in near real time to support the experiment operations. Light-
emitting diodes within the chamber can be used to illuminate the igniter and burner to both 
support the operations and provide reference images. The 12-bit digital camera records at up to 
30 full frames (1360x1024) per second, and is equipped with a motorized lens with independent 
control of the zoom, iris, and focus. The digital camera will be equipped with a filter assembly 
with four options, where selection of a clear “filter” allows for color imaging. Color imaging can 
also be carried out with a blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter, which balances the color planes to 
avoid saturation in the red while maintaining sensitivity in the blue and green. The natural flame 
color can be approximately reconstructed, but the primary purpose of the filter is pyrometry and 
measurement of the soot volume fraction, again via the techniques of [23-24]. A

measurement of the soot volume fraction, again via the techniques of [23-24]. Alternately, CH* 
imaging can be conducted with this camera because the filter assembly includes a 430-nm 
bandpass filter with a 10-nm full width at half-maximum transmission (FWHM). A 450-nm 
bandpass filter (again with a 10-nm FWHM) can be used with the CH* filter to effectively subtract 
interfering broadband soot emission. However, the filter assembly rotates slowly so such 
subtraction effectively requires a separate test with each filter and of course reproducible flame 
conditions. 
 
The video from the analog operations (i.e., ops) camera, also referred to as the internal camera, 
is not archived in space. The video is instead recorded on the ground in the operations center. Its 
gain was sometimes adjusted for improved imaging of dim flames, e.g., approaching extinction.

The sensitivity of the color digital camera, often referenced as the ACME DataCam (i.e., Data 
Camera), to the dim microgravity flames was such that it was often used with long exposure times 
and thus low framing rates, for example on the order of 1 frame per second. The clear “filter” is 
of fused silica. Unfortunately, the thickness of the blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter and the added 
antireflective (AR) coating caused too great a reduction in the red, so it does not balance the 
intensity of the three color planes as intended and thereby can limit the accuracy of temperature 
determination. Meanwhile, rather than the 450-nm bandpass filter described above, the high

For more information, see the Data Camera Characterization Report (ACME-RPT-010 Rev. A).

Pyrometry can alternately be accomplished with CIR’s monochrome High-Bit Depth Multispectral 
(HiBMs) camera, equipped with a Liquid-Crystal Tunable Filter (LCTF), which allows for imaging at 
multiple spectra, but requires a quasi-steady flame for measurement at each desired band. This 
camera has a telecentric optical system and is recorded at 512x512 and 30 frames per second 
(fps). Although it has a 1024x1024 pixel array, binning has been necessary because of signal loss 
through the LCTF. Both soot pyrometry and Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) are possible, where 
ACME is equipped with a crew-replaceable array of 5 silicon carbide (SiC) fibers. The fibers are 
orthogonal to the flame axis and the array can be translated along the flame axis to the desired 
position downstream of the burner, e.g., based on the downlink of the analog video. During set 
up, the crew can manually orient the array so that it is orthogonal to either ACME’s color digital 
camera or the HiBMs camera with the LCTF. An alternate fiber array including

enable determination of the soot volume fraction [24].

instead relied on use of ACME’s color DataCam for such temperature measurements. For an
