3. Tests Conducted 
This text is an excerpt from the “Results” section of the ACME/E-FIELD Flames – 30-Day Operation 
Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 (which is included in the ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final 
Report). 
 
A total of 219 flames were ignited for the E-FIELD Flames experiment, with 142 and 77 
respectively ignited during Increments 55-56 and 57-58. Note that the investigation’s testing was 
completed during Increment 57, so no flames were ignited during Increment 58. The first and 
second rounds of testing respectively occurred in March-May 2018 and September-November 
2018. The two rounds of tests resulted in 120 and 99 ignited flames conducted with coflow and 
gas-jet burners, respectively. The coflow burner was developed for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion 
Flame (CLD Flame) experiment, where CLD Flames’ second round occurred between the two 
rounds of the E-FIELD Flames experiment. The ‘interruption’ in the E-FIELD Flames testing was 
intentionally planned years in advance to enable the PI team

passages.id: PSI-22::PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf::p4::9
passages.docId: PSI-22::PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
passages.title: E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document
passages.text:
curred between the two 
rounds of the E-FIELD Flames experiment. The ‘interruption’ in the E-FIELD Flames testing was 
intentionally planned years in advance to enable the PI team to review the initial results in detail 
and with that knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize its scientific outcome. 
 
E-FIELD Flames does not have living subjects like a life science experiment, but the tests are 
independently conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene. Both are 
simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood. Methane (CH4) is the 
primary component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot given the absence of 
carbon-carbon bonds. Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is highly sooting because of its carbon 
double bond. For both fuels, tests were conducted with pure fuel and fuel mixed with nitrogen 
over a broad range of dilutions. For limited cases, the fuel and nitrogen was premixed on the 
ground prior to launch. ACME bottles were launched with methane concentrations of 30%, 40%, 
45%, and 100% with a balance of nitrogen

passages.text:
es, the fuel and nitrogen was premixed on the 
ground prior to launch. ACME bottles were launched with methane concentrations of 30%, 40%, 
45%, and 100% with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis). Similarly, bottles were launched 
with ethylene concentrations of 30%, 50%, and 100%, again with a balance of nitrogen (on a 
volume basis). But the ACME hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and nitrogen to 
the burner, allowing for on-orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of fuel concentrations. 
In all cases, the coflow was 21% oxygen with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis). 
 
No samples (e.g., of soot) were collected for E-FIELD Flames; all of the ISS results were 
electronically transmitted to the ground. That is furthermore the case for all currently planned 
ACME experiments.

4. Data Interpretation 
This key section provides (1) a general description of the raw experimental data and associated files and 
(2) guidance on data conversions, e.g., to engineering units. Only limited guidance is provided for the 
processing of image data, with the important exception of the conversion of the ACME DataCam images 
from the raw Halcon object (HOBJ) format. 
 
A. Non-Imaging Data 
Data and files discussed in this section include the following: 
Data Output File 
Mass Flow Controller (MFC) Setpoint File 
Fuel Oxidizer Management Assembly (FOMA) data 
Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS) data 
 
Some ACME experiments featured measurements made with the CIR’s Gas Chromatograph 
Instrumentation Package (GCIP), but it was not used for the E-FIELD Flames experiment and a such 
that data type is not addressed in this document. 
 
1. Data Output File 
The basic ACME non-imaging measurements for each test are together in a file described in 
Section 8.1 Data Output File on page 124 of Software Interface D

1. Data Output File 
The basic ACME non-imaging measurements for each test are together in a file described in 
Section 8.1 Data Output File on page 124 of Software Interface Design Description (ACME-
DOC-010 Rev D). The test number is made up of the year (2-digts), day of year (3 digits), and 
test (a letter and single-digit number). As such, the example, 18073A3 is test A3 conducted 
on the 73rd day of 2018. But the test could also be early on the next (e.g., 74th) day because 
the day portion of ACME test numbers is not changed when operations continue past 
midnight (whether GMT or Eastern) into the start of the next day. 
 
Tests numbers that only differ by the final digit (e.g., 18073A1, 18073A2, and 18073A3) are 
normally similar and occasionally identical, where the number is indicative of the variant or 
repeat. Letters I and O are not used because of their similarity to 1 and 0. While initially used 
in ACME testing, the letter E ceased to be used because Excel software (for example) by 
default interpreted it as representing an exponential which was inconvenient. As a

passages.id: PSI-22::PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf::p6::15
passages.docId: PSI-22::PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
passages.title: E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document
passages.text:
y used 
in ACME testing, the letter E ceased to be used because Excel software (for example) by 
default interpreted it as representing an exponential which was inconvenient. As a related 
aside, ACME tests are often not conducted in order and some planned tests are regularly not 
conducted at all. The latter results in additional letter gaps if the tests from a day are sorted 
alphabetically. However, ACME testing often begins with test A1, where the final digit begins 
with 1 and is increased from there with variant or repeat tests for the same letter. 
 
The basic data is in a CSV format, i.e., with comma-separated values, which can be opened by 
spreadsheet software such as Microsoft Excel. The first row is a header and provides a limited 
summary of the hardware and operational conditions. The header is explained in Section 10.1 
Metadata Header of ACME-DOC-010 Rev D, which begins on page 126.

Additional conversion is required for the measurements of the gas flow rates found in second 
through fourth columns of the data file. By column (e.g., in Excel), the flow rates are for: 
 B MFCA1StaticMixerFlow oxidizer (or inert) gas 
 C MFCA2BypassFlow nitrogen 
 D MFCA3FuelFlow fuel 
 
The ACME MFCs are Hastings HFC-D-302 with default standard temperature and pressures 
(STP) of 0 Celsius and 760 torr for computations of volumetric flow or velocity. It is very 
important to understand that slpm, i.e., standard liters per minute, is a measurement of the 
mass (or alternatively molar) flow rate which is independent of the actual temperature or 
pressure. This is discussed for example in the MFC manual, where chapter 9 (on page 39) is 
“Volumetric vs. Mass Flow.” 
 
Conversions for the actual gases can be made with information provided in the manual on 
subsequent pages and the spreadsheets GasDataTables.xls and Inside gas mix calculator.xls 
which were both provided by the MFC manufacturer. First, open GasDataTables.xls

Computation of gas velocities, for example for the gas-jet and coflow burners, depends on 
burner dimensions. For the coflow burner, ACME mechanical design engineer Adrian Drake 
indicated the following: 
 
“The inner diameter of the inner tube is .085 inches. Its cross sectional area is .00567 
in^2, or 3.66 x 10^-6 m^2. 
 
The flow of the outer tube is a little tricky to calculate, based on where and how you 
measure. There’s an internal step in the outer tube that can’t be seen from outside, and 
blocks

passages.text:
flow of the outer tube is a little tricky to calculate, based on where and how you 
measure. There’s an internal step in the outer tube that can’t be seen from outside, and 
blocks the flow to the outer honeycombs. Because of this, when we calculated the cross-
sectional are of the outer tube, it measures from the inner step. 
 
The outer tube’s outer diameter at that step is 0.984 inches. Its cross section area at that 
diameter is .7605 in^2. From this we have to subtract the inner tube’s outer 
diameter: .095 inch diameter, so area is .00709. Subtract from the Outer Diameter and 
we get .7534 in^2, or .000486 m^2.”

3. Fuel Oxidizer Management Assembly (FOMA) data 
Relevant pressure, temperature, etc. data from the CIR is not found in the data output file 
discussed in section 4.A.1 of this document. Instead, it is found in 1-Hz files with names such 
as 18073A3_ACME_CAM3_Exposures.txt which are again in a comma-separated values (CSV) 
format despite the misleading txt suffix. As such, these files can be opened with standard 
spreadsheet software. 
 
Columns A and B (e.g., in Excel) both include timestamps, which can slightly differ (e.g., by a 
second), where column A is from the Image Processing and Storage Unit for Gigabit ethernet 
cameras (IPSU-G, which is also referred to as IPSU-5). The IPSU-G was used to record the

1. Analog, internal, operations (ops) camera 
This color analog camera is mounted on the ACME chamber insert, and as such is within the 
combustion chamber and is sometimes referred to as the internal camera. Its primary 
purpose is to support the operations, e.g., to visualize the burner and igniter, and as such is

but is streamed to the ground in near real time and is recorded on CIR consoles at the Glenn 
ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC) in a Transport Stream (TS) format using VLC Media 
Player which can be freely downloaded from https://www.videolan.org/vlc/. That software 
has a snapshot function allowing for convenient extraction of still images, e.g., for making 
measurements of flame dimensions. 
 
2. ACME Data Camera (DataCam) 
ACME’s primary camera is a high-definition (1360 x 1024), 12-bit color camera mounted 
outside the chamber on CIR’s optical bench. It is equipped with a motorized lens with 
independent control of the zoom, iris, and focus. It has a filter barrel with a fused silica 
window (for color imaging), a blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter, and bandpass filters for 
imaging CH* and HCHO (formaldehyde) chemiluminescence.

1. Introduction 
The narrative description of the experimental procedure is from the ‘Methods / Experimental’ section of 
the following conference paper: 
Y.-C. Chien, J. Tinajero, D. Stocker, U. Hegde, and D. Dunn-Rankin, “Electric Field Effects on Flames in 
Microgravity on the International Space Station,” 2018 Spring Technical Meeting of the Central States 
Section of The Combustion Institute, Minneapolis, MN, 20-22 May 2018. 
This description also appears in Section 4.B Overview of Experiment Test Operations of the E-FIELD Flames 
Final Report. Note that the referenced Figure 4 (showing the coflow burner geometry) is not included in 
this document. 
 
The CIR experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. Thus far, ACME’s activity has 
included the majority of the crew members, regardless of their nationalities. Most often the astronauts 
and cosmonauts exchange gas bottles, mass flow controllers, and igniter tips. In the latter case, the igniter 
tip exchange can occur after failure or proactively be

passages.title: E-FIELD Flames procedure 20200723
passages.text:
he astronauts 
and cosmonauts exchange gas bottles, mass flow controllers, and igniter tips. In the latter case, the igniter 
tip exchange can occur after failure or proactively before failure when the crew already has changes to 
make changes in the interior of the insert. While these activities may seem mundane, the crew play a 
critical role in setting up the hardware for each experiment. As an extreme example, there were crew 
activities on 8 separate days in Sept.-Oct. 2017 to configure the CIR and ACME hardware for the first ACME 
experiment, namely the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment. In contrast, only two 
crew days were required to reconfigure the hardware for the first E-FIELD Flames tests because of the 
initial use of the same coflow burner. Planning is critical because crew activity is scheduled three weeks 
in advance, for which detailed procedures must be prepared and uplinked to the ISS. 
 
All CIR tests are remotely commanded from the ground from NASA’s Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center 
(GIPOC) in Cleveland, Ohio. Typically, four to six peopl

linked to the ISS. 
 
All CIR tests are remotely commanded from the ground from NASA’s Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center 
(GIPOC) in Cleveland, Ohio. Typically, four to six people staff four consoles during the testing. The CIR 
hardware is controlled from the Rack Officer (RO) and Data Management Officer (DMO) consoles, and the 
ACME hardware is controlled from the Payload Developer (PD) console. Two shifts of personnel are 
scheduled to staff these three consoles on test days because they typically last 14 hours with the many 
pre- and post-testing activities. Given that the tests are remotely commanded, the operations are carried 
out in the day and evening in Cleveland, e.g., from 7 AM to 9 PM. A day’s tests, i.e., with flames, are 
normally conducted in a period of 10 hours of less. Tests are normally conducted on three weekdays per 
two weeks. On intervening weekdays, the image data is downlinked and the crew often swap one or both 
gas bottles. Transferring and downlinking data from a day’s tests also requires a 2-shift day for the RO 
and DMO consoles, where it is always ne

passages.title: E-FIELD Flames procedure 20200723
passages.text:
d the crew often swap one or both 
gas bottles. Transferring and downlinking data from a day’s tests also requires a 2-shift day for the RO 
and DMO consoles, where it is always necessary to verify that data was downlinked without errors and 
that data is not missing. Those two positions are also staffed to guide and oversee the crew activity. As 
a result, the CIR consoles are normally actively staffed on four weekdays per week. A team of four carry 
out the detailed planning for the CIR and ACME console staff, and the daily operational plans typically 
exceed 50 pages on days including testing. 
 
The science console allows for review of the analog video and non-imaging telemetry (at 1 Hz) in near real 
time but doesn’t allow for commanding. In the case of E-FIELD Flames, arrangements were made so that 
the analog video is streamed to a secure computer at UC Irvine to allow the research team to participate 
in test operations and to recommend adjustments to the day’s planned parameters. That team does not 
see the telemetry during the testing, but is in communication via phone and

passages.title: E-FIELD Flames procedure 20200723
passages.text:
e 
in test operations and to recommend adjustments to the day’s planned parameters. That team does not 
see the telemetry during the testing, but is in communication via phone and e-mail with their NASA 
research partners at the GRC ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). While there are many preparatory 
steps, the tests are ultimately conducted using an uploaded software script and parameter files. In 
advance of the test day, the UC Irvine science team plans the nearly 60 parameters in the voltage sweep 
script and specifies other parameters that are configured outside of the script, such as camera settings.

passages.title: E-FIELD Flames procedure 20200723
passages.text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Experimental Procedure 23 July 2020 
3 
 
It is also possible to effectively conduct tests in a ‘manual’ mode, where parameters are changed in 
response to the analog video downlink or telemetry. For example, the electric field potential can be 
adjusted to approach a stability or soot limit. 
 
Typically, ten E-FIELD Flames tests are conducted per test day. Despite the short test durations, the low 
rate results from several unavoidable factors. After a test is conducted, the 125-Hz non-imaging data is 
downlinked for immediate review by the science team. A small sample of images are often downlinked 
to ensure that the camera exposures are appropriate, where the times for those images are typically 
selected based on non-imaging data to provide extreme examples. The review helps to verify parameters 
or plan for adjustments in subsequent tests, e.g., to select the voltage range after determining where the 
ion current saturates for the given flame conditions. After a test is conducted, a fan circulates the chamber 
atmosphere after which the chamber is vented (t

passages.title: E-FIELD Flames procedure 20200723
passages.text:
etermining where the 
ion current saturates for the given flame conditions. After a test is conducted, a fan circulates the chamber 
atmosphere after which the chamber is vented (to space) back to atmospheric pressure, if needed. 
Midway through a day’s E-FIELD Flames tests, the atmosphere is circulated for 15 minutes through a filter 
cartridge filled with molecular sieves to capture any soot and adsorb at least a portion of the combustion 
products, e.g., carbon dioxide, water vapor, and incomplete combustion products. The tests are only 
conducted when both Ku and S band communication is available through NASA’s Tracking and Data Relay 
Satellite (TDRS) System. Depending on the various orbits, there are periodic communication outages with 
a loss of signal (LOS) that can be a short handover (from one satellite to another) or can last as long as 30 
minutes. 
 
A variety of constraints limit the number of tests that can be performed, both overall and on a daily basis. 
The next combustion experiments in the CIR will feature solid fuels and focus on flame spread and material 
flamma

passages.title: E-FIELD Flames procedure 20200723
passages.text:
tests that can be performed, both overall and on a daily basis. 
The next combustion experiments in the CIR will feature solid fuels and focus on flame spread and material 
flammability. That follow-on plan limits the duration of ACME operations, where each ACME experiment 
is allotted four months for testing. Although it requires additional crew time, these allotments are split 
into two rounds so that the investigators have a break from testing for careful review of the early results 
so that they can maximize the scientific outcome of their second round. This paper reports on early results 
from the first round of E-FIELD Flames. 
 
While nitrogen is available from the space station, the combustion testing is limited by the available gas 
bottles that were and are launched to support the tests. For E-FIELD Flames and most of ACME’s 
experiments, the test matrices used to plan those gas resources were established in 2010. At that time, 
NASA limited the scope of the ACME tests matrices with the intent of focused experiments with limited 
objectives rather than comprehensive experi

passages.title: E-FIELD Flames procedure 20200723
passages.text:
tablished in 2010. At that time, 
NASA limited the scope of the ACME tests matrices with the intent of focused experiments with limited 
objectives rather than comprehensive experiments. As such, the general target was 50 tests per 
experiment. For most ACME experiments, the limiting gas constraint is the oxygen/nitrogen bottles used 
to fill the chamber. This resource constraint is exacerbated by the CIR because it is equipped with a pair 
of redundant safety timers to limit the fuel that can flow into the combustion chamber (where the timers 
can be set for the oxidizer flow in the case of inverse flame testing). The timers can only be reset by 
venting the combustion chamber. Therefore, the timer limit combined with other constraints effectively 
corresponds to the day’s maximum flow time for the fuel (or more generally, the limiting reactant). For 
E-FIELD Flames, the safety timers are set to the maximum value of 999 seconds, which corresponds to the 
10 tests typically completed per day. 
 
Another constraint is the available time in a day, where the console personnel and ISS re

passages.title: E-FIELD Flames procedure 20200723
passages.text:
m value of 999 seconds, which corresponds to the 
10 tests typically completed per day. 
 
Another constraint is the available time in a day, where the console personnel and ISS resources, such as 
the video downlink, are planned for a limited number of hours. When necessary for the research, NASA 
does have continuous 24-hour/day operations for some non-CIR experiments. But as discussed, the ACME 
tests are typically two minutes or less in duration, so the testing is almost always limited to the planned 
durations.

passages.title: E-FIELD Flames procedure 20200723
passages.text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Experimental Procedure 23 July 2020 
4 
 
Data limits are yet another constraint, where the on-orbit hardware can store a limited amount of data. 
More importantly, 127,000 MB is the most that can be reasonably managed in a two-shift transfer and 
downlink day. Therefore, tests days are limited to this amount of data, where image data from select 
cameras is often archived at reduced rates to mitigate this challenge. Nonetheless, the limit sometimes 
forces decisions to abandon recorded images. 
 
This detailed description of operations and hardware provides the context under which the ACME 
experiments are conducted. Their complexity makes the flame conditions seem trivial in comparison. It 
is a simple coflow flame, with just a small jet of fuel surrounded by a weak coflow of ‘air’ which also fills 
the chamber, but where tests are also conducted with no coflow. A test includes starting the gas flows to 
prime the system, energizing the igniter to initiate a flame, retracting the igniter, and allowing the flame 
to steady slightly before energizing the electric

passages.title: E-FIELD Flames procedure 20200723
passages.text:
g the gas flows to 
prime the system, energizing the igniter to initiate a flame, retracting the igniter, and allowing the flame 
to steady slightly before energizing the electric field to its initial value. The flame is again allowed to 
steady before beginning a voltage sweep over a specified range with steps or smooth ramps of specified 
voltage changes and durations. The sweep can be in one direction or can include cycles of sweeps. After 
each test, a duplicate field sweep is made to ensure that there are no current leaks, i.e., other than the 
ion current through the flame. 
 
The first phase tests in E-FIELD Flames employ the coflow burner geometry shown in Figure 4, with the 
fuel tube extending slightly above the burner surface. The results shown in this paper are for tests 
conducted with 100% methane in a chamber atmosphere and coflow (when used) of synthetic ‘air’ (i.e., 
21/79 oxygen/nitrogen by volume) at a nominal pressure of 100 kPa. The mesh is held at a negative 
potential relative to the burner in these tests. The sweeps shown in this paper extend to at least -7 kV

passages.title: E-FIELD Flames procedure 20200723
passages.text:

potential relative to the burner in these tests. The sweeps shown in this paper extend to at least -7 kV, 
where the voltage is increased in small steps (e.g., of 100 V) lasting 1-2 seconds. The details of the voltage 
changes can be seen in the resulting plots.

5 
 
2. Test Sequences and ParametersAll E-FIELD Flames tests conducted on the ISS 
were carried out using automated software which had its roots in ACME’s Integrated Science 
Requirements Documents (ISRD, RDR version, Rev. B) and Science Operations Requirements 
Documents (SORD, Rev. A). The E-FIELD Flames Science Requirements Document (SRD) is of course 
pertinent but only that which was incorporated in the ISRD and SORD was used by the engineering 
team in developing the control software. 
 
Multiple software scripts and corresponding parameter files were prepared to address the various 
objectives explained in this excerpt from section 4.2 of the ACME ISRD. The section is fully included with 
the important exception of the tables detailing the envisioned operational sequences. Given that they 
were conceptual, they were left out to reduce the chance of a confused understanding of the engineering 
implementation. For example, excessive electromagnetic interference (EMI) led to a change in the design 
of the electric field sy

passages.title: E-FIELD Flames procedure 20200723
passages.text:
ce of a confused understanding of the engineering 
implementation. For example, excessive electromagnetic interference (EMI) led to a change in the design 
of the electric field system limiting the voltage to a single polarity on a given test day. As a result, the step 
response procedure could not be carried out as detailed in Table 4.2.2 of the ISRD. 
 
The E-FIELD experiment consists of 4 objectives corresponding to 4 series of tests using 2 different 
diffusion flame burner configurations. The first three test series provide the key fundamental 
information regarding the electrical character of diffusion flames and the influence of electric fields on 
soot formation; the final series focuses on electric field sensing and control of flames. 
 
General Operations 
Before any of the electric field experiments, the high voltage mesh should be installed (or moved into 
position). Leak current should be measured by sweeping the voltage from 0 to 10kV and 0 to -10kV 
with no flame present. A steep rise in current under these conditions indicates corona discharge and 
sets the upper limi

passages.title: E-FIELD Flames procedure 20200723
passages.text:
red by sweeping the voltage from 0 to 10kV and 0 to -10kV 
with no flame present. A steep rise in current under these conditions indicates corona discharge and 
sets the upper limit on the potential. The test sequence involves a complete repeat voltage sweep 
with no flame to provide a point-by-point current leak measurement. A similar sweep should be 
completed following flame extinguishment at the end of a test set. Only ion current would need to be 
measured during the no-flame sweep. In addition, excessive leak current at relatively low voltage may 
indicate electron emission from carbon buildup on the gas jet flame tip. If the leak current exceeds 
10% of the flame ion current, cleaning of the gas jet tip is requested. Cleaning consists of a manual 
wiping or possibly burning off the carbon with a modified flame condition. We expect this to be a rare 
request, but the continuous monitor of flameless ion current provides a reliable in-situ monitor. We 
assume that the chamber will be emptied and refilled approximately every 7-8 tests to minimize the 
oxygen concentration uncertai

passages.title: E-FIELD Flames procedure 20200723
passages.text:
n current provides a reliable in-situ monitor. We 
assume that the chamber will be emptied and refilled approximately every 7-8 tests to minimize the 
oxygen concentration uncertainty in the test chamber. The exact times for settling and voltage steps 
may vary (they should be reconfigurable from the ground), but a nominal expected operational 
sequence for one chamber fill and the key measurement data sets are shown below. 
 
(A) Voltage Sweep – collection of VI curves (or VCC curves) -- where the voltage is swept from 0-±5kV 
(or until flame blowout) and the ion current is monitored and recorded. The sweep will consist of a 
series of discrete steps, where a settling time is allowed after each voltage change. At the same time, 
color and OH* video records the flame shape and luminosity (both broadband flame and soot 
luminosity and OH* chemiluminescence) throughout the sweep. A typical step sweep might comprise: 
15 second ignition & stabilization; 100 V/step, 0.3 sec settle between steps, and a 0.25 sec. ion current 
measurement at each point, to ±5kV or blowout. Blowout can be de

passages.title: E-FIELD Flames procedure 20200723
passages.text:
mprise: 
15 second ignition & stabilization; 100 V/step, 0.3 sec settle between steps, and a 0.25 sec. ion current 
measurement at each point, to ±5kV or blowout. Blowout can be detected by a sharp drop in ion 
current. Expected run time is 50 seconds per sweep (not including a background current sweep with 
the flame off). However, the time between voltage steps for flame adjustment and data collection 
shall be adjustable via uplink between the values of 0-10 seconds.

passages.title: E-FIELD Flames procedure 20200723
passages.text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Experimental Procedure 23 July 2020 
6 
 
 
(B) Step Response—This test will involve the rapid change of voltage from a base level to a much 
higher (or lower) level, while the ion current (and flame luminosity and shape) is monitored in time 
as it settles to its new steady value. The key measurable is the ion current as a function of time through 
the voltage step change and the flame’s subsequent settling. As in test set (A), video, luminosity, and 
chemiluminescence will record flame behaviors in response to an instantaneous change in the electric 
field. A typical experiment sequence might comprise a 15 second ignition and stabilization, step 
changes on the order of hundreds of volts, and recording ion current for 2 seconds between step 
changes (where steps will not be limited to a single polarity). Settling time for these step changes in 
zero gravity (particularly, for soot related phenomena) may need to be adjusted via uplink; the test 
procedures shown are based on a nominal settling time observed in preliminary testing at 1g and the 
2.2 Second Drop To

passages.title: E-FIELD Flames procedure 20200723
passages.text:
ted phenomena) may need to be adjusted via uplink; the test 
procedures shown are based on a nominal settling time observed in preliminary testing at 1g and the 
2.2 Second Drop Tower. The range of times between voltage steps may vary between 0-100 seconds. 
 
(C) Electric Field Effects on Soot – The following tests will demonstrate the effects of electric fields on 
soot (measured by broadband emission from the flame and soot volume fraction) by slowly increasing 
the coflow air velocity, comparing the flame structure at each step to a flame affected purely by 
electric forcing. Conditions will be uplinked and derived from experiments (A) and (B). Timing will 
depend on the burner, but each test will be allowed at least 100 seconds. Also, note that the step 
time between one coflow velocitity and the next shall be adjustable via uplink between the values of 
0-10 seconds. Broad solid angle collection luminosity, flame images along with soot volume fraction 
and soot pyrometry will be collected. 
 
(D) Open Loop Sensing and Control – The experiments associated with control will be up

passages.title: E-FIELD Flames procedure 20200723
passages.text:
osity, flame images along with soot volume fraction 
and soot pyrometry will be collected. 
 
(D) Open Loop Sensing and Control – The experiments associated with control will be uplinked, based 
on the results of the above baseline mapping experiments (A) and (B) above. Timing will depend on 
the condition, but each test will be allowed at least 70 seconds. The procedure is a series of voltage 
ramps (or small steps with continuous data collection). Ion current and luminosity (broadband and 
CH*) fluctuations will be collected as well as flame images. The time between voltage changes for 
flame adjustment and data collection shall be adjustable via uplink between the values of 0-10 
seconds. 
 
Although four types of E-FIELD Flames tests are discussed above, it was determined by 2017 that three 
types of tests could be used to address the four experimental objectives, where a separate script to 
investigate effects on the soot was not needed. 
 
While scripts were developed for the three remaining sequences, it was later determined that the open 
loop objectives could be accomplished

passages.title: E-FIELD Flames procedure 20200723
passages.text:
effects on the soot was not needed. 
 
While scripts were developed for the three remaining sequences, it was later determined that the open 
loop objectives could be accomplished by proper selection of parameter values with the voltage sweep 
script, e.g., limiting the voltage range. Furthermore, the step response script was ultimately not employed 
because of the slow response time of the high-voltage power supply. As such, all of the experiment’s 
flame tests were conducted with the voltage sweep script. Therefore, that procedure is the only one to 
be further discussed in this document.

lines represent the oxidizer coflow (if any), nitrogen flow (if any), and fuel flow. The gold lines represent 
optional changes to flow rates, e.g., for a change in the fuel dilution after ignition. The phases are 
described in detail at the bottom of the schematic, where the nomenclature throughout the figure 
generally corresponds to parameter names.

18 May 2020 
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) 
Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) 
ACME/E-FIELD Flames - Impacts, Benefits, and Products 
 Prepared by Dennis Stocker, ACME Project Scientist, dennis.p.stocker@nasa.gov, 216-433-2166 
 
Impacts, Benefits, and Products 
This text is the ‘Impacts, Benefits, and Products’ section from the 2019 version of the final report. 
 
The impact of this work is, as the original objectives identified, the delivery of a unique data set of chemi-
ion behavior in flames under sufficiently stable and symmetric conditions that models and theories can 
be evaluated against the results. As an example, the very distinctive shape of the V-I curve in microgravity, 
when matched in models, will give a very good indication that the feedback between ion driven wind and 
changes in flame shape and burning behavior that then further change the ion current is captured 
accurately. 
 
These results have already garnered the interest of other groups working on electric field effects on 
flames. 
 
The use of elec

passages.title: E-FIELD Flames benefits 20200518
passages.text:
change the ion current is captured 
accurately. 
 
These results have already garnered the interest of other groups working on electric field effects on 
flames. 
 
The use of electric field effects on flames can be as sensor (variations of ion current as associated with 
combustion behavior) or actuator (ion-driven wind changes the flame shape and characteristics). This 
work, as was originally planned, provides quantitative evaluation of the sensing and response potential of 
electric fields in combustion. The applications can include the control of flames. 
 
Patents 
Thus far, no patents have resulted from the E-FIELD Flames research.

30-day Operational Accomplishments Report

ACME Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments 
E-FIELD Flames Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames 
E-FIELD Flames is one of several independent experiments that are part of the ACME project, 
which uses a single modular set of hardware to carry out studies of flames burning gaseous fuels 
in the ISS’ Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). 
 
Prepared by the PI team and Dennis Stocker (dennis.p.stocker@nasa.gov), the ACME Project 
Scientist, who is the primary contact for E-FIELD Flames and ACME information. 
 
 
 
Principal Investigator (PI): Prof. Derek Dunn-Rankin, University of California, Irvine, CA 
PI project scientist: Dr. Yu-Chien (Alice) Chien, University of California, Irvine, CA 
Lead collaborator: Prof. Sergey Minaev, Far Eastern Federal University, Vladivostok, 
Russia

I. Introduction 
The Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment is conducted 
in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the 
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. In this experiment, an 
electric field with voltages as high as 10,000 volts is established between the burner and a flat, 
circular mesh electrode suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner. The motion of the 
charged ions, which are naturally produced within the flame, are strongly affected by a strong 
electric field. The resulting ion-driven wind can dramatically influence the stability and sooting 
behavior of the flame. Measurements are made of electric-field strength, the ion current passing 
through the flame, an

passages.text:
n wind can dramatically influence the stability and sooting 
behavior of the flame. Measurements are made of electric-field strength, the ion current passing 
through the flame, and flame characteristics such as the size, structure, temperature, soot, and 
stability. Conducting the tests in microgravity allows for great simplifications in the analysis of 
ion-driven convection and flame interaction, enabling new understanding and the development 
of less polluting and more efficient combustion technology for use on Earth. 
 
An electric field can strongly influence flames because of its effect on the ions produced as a 
result of the combustion reactions. The induced ion wind can modify the flame shape, alter the 
soot and stability limits, and direct the heat transfer. The purpose of the E-FIELD Flames

ACME/E-FIELD Flames – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 
 
2 
 
experiment is to gain an improved understanding of flame ion production and learn how the 
electric field can be used to manipulate the ions and control non-premixed flames for practical 
benefit. For example, electric fields can enable stable burner operation at fuel-lean conditions 
with reduced pollutant emission, i.e., where the flame is not reliably sustained without the 
electric field. As another example, the role of electric fields on soot formation can be dramatic. 
It appears that the ion driven wind alters the local convection and strongly influences the 
residence time of the soot precursors within the hot flame. The experiment contributes to our 
critical understanding of combustion processes in the presence of electric fields. 
 
More specifically, E-FIELD Flames has the following experimental objectives: 
A. Determine the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as 
functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and the amount of inert

jectives: 
A. Determine the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as 
functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and the amount of inert 
(nitrogen) in the fuel. 
B. Obtain the time response of the flame chemiluminescence, luminosity, and the ion 
current to large step changes in voltage, as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) 
flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream. 
C. Evaluate and manipulate sooting behavior (i.e., soot volume fraction and location of 
luminous soot) in relation to the electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions 
of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to 
the fuel stream. 
D. Use the variation of the chemi-ion current as a function of applied voltage to characterize 
the combustion behavior of near-limit lifted flames and use the associated ion-driven 
wind to stabilize or reattach these flames. 
 
The effect of the electric field on the flame is studied through tests conducted with a range of 
flame and electric field conditio

The effect of the electric field on the flame is studied through tests conducted with a range of 
flame and electric field conditions. The fuel, fuel jet velocity, air flow, electric-field voltage and 
polarity are the primary parameters of the E-FIELD Flames experiment. Tests are conducted with 
methane and ethylene, including nitrogen dilutions of each, which provide a broad range of soot-
producing conditions, i.e., from soot-free to highly sooting. They are conducted with both a 
simple gas-jet burner and the coflow burner that was also used for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion 
Flame (CLD Flame) experiment. Tests with the coflow burner is conducted with and without a 
coflow of air, where the results of the latter are compared with those from the gas-jet burner to 
assess the effect of air entrainment on the flame. The coflow burner also provides a different 
electrode configuration (close to a plane-to-plane) than the jet burner (close to a point-to-plane). 
In a typical test, the mesh electrode is energized at increasing potentials

passages.text:
electrode configuration (close to a plane-to-plane) than the jet burner (close to a point-to-plane). 
In a typical test, the mesh electrode is energized at increasing potentials (relative to the burner), 
where the flame’s response (e.g., ion current, luminosity, shape) to the resulting field strength is 
measured. The field strength is changed in repeated steps or is instead smoothly ramped. 
 
Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages 
over normal-gravity studies. For example, the flicker of flames, which is a buoyancy-driven (i.e., 
gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. 
Microgravity flame flicker is then the result of electric body forces alone. Length scales are 
increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum-
dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be studied at low

velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to 
their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-gravity flames 
because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity 
flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free. The 
absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability 
behavior where chemical kinetics are important. With these advantages, microgravity testing 
can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the 
gravitational environment of the combustion application. Chemi-ion species, electronically 
excited chemiluminescent species are are very low concentration in typical flames, making the 
reduced buoyancy environment valuable for evaluating the minor species chemistry.

II. Methods/Research Operations 
 
A. Discussion of Method/Protocol 
E-FIELD Flames and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the 
ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. 
The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack 
(CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. 
 
All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload 
Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a 
nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. However, it may alternately 
be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in 
response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry 
stream. For example, the mesh voltage can be adjusted to approach a flame’s stability or 
soot limit. This was not done during Increments 55-56, where the

passages.text:
ailable in the telemetry 
stream. For example, the mesh voltage can be adjusted to approach a flame’s stability or 
soot limit. This was not done during Increments 55-56, where the console commanding 
during a test was typically limited to halting the test when it was observed in the analog 
ops video that the flame had extinguished. 
 
Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to 
ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. 
 
Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary 
analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing. 
 
 
III. Results 
A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight 
A total of 142 flames were ignited for the E-FIELD Flames experiment during Increments 
55 and 56. The first round of testing occurred from March to May 2018, which was 
followed by a second round, which began in September 2018 and was still underway at 
the beginning of Increment 57. The first round of tests resulted in 120 ignited flames

Flame) experiment, where CLD Flames’s second round occurred between the two rounds 
of the E-FIELD Flames expeirment. The ‘interruption’ in the E-FIELD Flames testing was 
intentionally planned years in advance to enable the PI team to review the initial results 
in detail and with that knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize its scientific 
outcome. 
 
E-FIELD Flames does not have living subjects like a life science experiment, but the tests 
are independently conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene. 
Both are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood. Methane 
(CH4) is the primary component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot 
given the absence of carbon-carbon bonds. Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is highly sooting 
because of its carbon double bond. For both fuels, tests were conducted with pure fuel

which is used for CLD Flame with a narrow bandpass filter to image CH* 
chemiluminesence. Use of the IPSU-G was recovered by astronaut Scott Tingle on

only intermittently operable in mid-Sept. 2018 and was not operable at the start of E-
FIELD Flames’ second round. Those capabilities were not seen as critical for E-FIELD 
Flames, where the illumination is significantly blocked by the mounting bracket for 
the mesh electrode. Therefore, the tests on Sept. 26 (18269) and Oct. 1 (18274) were 
conducted without HiBMs imaging or the CIR illumination. It was later determined to 
be an issue with a cable connection, which was corrected by astronaut Alex Gerst on 
Oct. 22 (18295) when he carried out other ACME tasks.

result, there is little lost other than the time in the failed test attempt. The aborts 
normally occur because of communication issues with IPSU-1. These are infrequent, 
but there are some days when tests abort repeatedly. 
 
Tests are of course also unsuccessful when the flame fails to ignite. The first test of 
the day has sometimes failed to ignite, presumably because the fuel line has not been 
sufficiently primed. Ignition is sometimes unsuccessful because the settings for the 
automatic flame detection are such that detection threshold is reached because of 
the igniter glow rather than a flame. As a result of the detection, the hot-wire igniter 
is deactivated and retracted, which is of course an issue if the flame has yet to ignite. 
This is typically avoided by detecting ignition with measurement of the flame’s OH* 
chemiluminescence with a Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) module. The OH* 
chemiluminescence, in the ultraviolet at 31

flame rather than the glowing igniter, which emits primarily in the infrared and visible 
spectrum. However, the combination of igniter settings and PMT gains can lead to 
false ignition detection.

if it is sticking in a few places, where the flow rate won’t linearly ramp when

C. Completeness/Quality of Data 
The number of flames ignited significantly exceeds the planned tests which were (1) 
specified as required in the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD), 
using the gas-jet burner, and (2) later expanded to include tests with the coflow burner 
to partially make up for science loss resulting from the slow response time of the high-
voltage power supply. Following the revision, a total of 74 E-FIELD Flames tests were 
identified as required. In contrast, 120 flames were ignited in the experiment’s first 
round, i.e., first half. In that round, roughly 200% more flames were ignited than had 
been planned.

discussed in section III.B, the IPSU-1 was not working at the beginning of the second round 
of testing, preventing use of both the HiBMs camera and the CIR’s collimated illumination 
package. Those are not critical for E-FIELD Flames, so tests continued without their use.

Data from the E-FIELD Flames experiments includes video recordings from the operations 
camera for general flame behavior, the ACME data camera for high resolution images at 
various exposures and frame rates as dictated by the flame luminosity, intensified camera 
images and non-imaging data at 100 Hz. The non-imaging data is extracted using Matlab 
scripts (modified from those developed by CLD Flame researchers) to show trends of ion 
current and flame luminosity as a function of the applied field, and the flame pa

The overall data volume is large with a storage limit of 127,000 MB per test day, the data 
has been downloaded to the hard drive with a backup system at UC Irvine. At this stage, 
with operations ongoing, the analysis is comparative and qualitative, just to show the 
major differences in behavior in microgravity and normal-gravity (1-g) flames.

distinct maximum of ion current for co-flow burner flames in microgravity, where the 1-g 
flames more smoothly reach a saturation condition. The results also show that the

provides a measure of combustion performance in that ion production is a function of

(1) The ion current reaches a peak at approximately the same field strength for both 
velocities in 1-g while in microgravity the ion current peak for a lower fuel velocity 
occurs at a lower field strength. The field strength at the peak current seems to scale 
linearly with the fuel velocity. 
 
 
Figure 5. Ion current as a function of field strength and fuel velocity with no coflow in 
normal gravity. (a) 16 cm/s methane. (b) 19 cm/s methane. 
 
(2) In microgravity, the ion current does not smoothly increase to saturation nor does it 
show a gentle peak with a mild decrease as is seen in the normal gravity results. 
Instead, in microgravity there is a distinct peak in the ion current with a severe 
decrease throughout the saturation condition, with a final saturation plateau 
observed at voltages substantially above the voltage at peak ion current. That is, the 
microgravity final saturation is not the maximum ion current observed. This 
difference is more dramatic when there is n

passages.text:
tially above the voltage at peak ion current. That is, the 
microgravity final saturation is not the maximum ion current observed. This 
difference is more dramatic when there is no coflow, which suggests that entrainment 
plays an important role whether caused by buoyancy or a forced coflow. 
 
(3) The peak ion current is higher for microgravity than comparison 1-g flames. The 
reason is not obvious at this point but may result from a more focused upward flow 
from the electric body force and ion-driven wind as compared to the combined effects 
of the ion wind and buoyancy. 
 
(4) The peak ion current is approximately proportional to fuel flow velocity, which, as 
described in prior studies, reflects the relationship between ion production and the 
carbon flux into the system. The peak ion current also increases with the coflow which 
suggests that healthier oxidizer transport helps increase the ion production.

1 June 2019 
30-day Operational Accomplishments Report 
… for the International Space Station (ISS) Increments 57 and 58 
 
ACME Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments 
E-FIELD Flames Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames 
E-FIELD Flames is one of several independent experiments that are part of the ACME project, 
which uses a single modular set of hardware to carry out studies of flames burning gaseous fuels 
in the ISS’ Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). The investigation was carried out in two rounds of 
tests, where the first (with ACME’s coflow burner) occurred in Increment 55 and the second (with 
a gas-jet burner) began in Increment 56 and ended in Increment 57. As a result, there is nothing 
to be reported for Increment 58. 
 
Prepared by the PI team and Dennis Stocker (dennis.p.stocker@nasa.gov), the ACME Project 
Scientist, who is the primary contact for E-FIELD Flames and ACME information. 
 
 
 
Principal Investigator (PI): Prof. Derek Dunn-Rankin, Univ

I. Introduction 
The Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment was 
conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of 
the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. In this experiment, an 
electric field with voltages as high as 10,000 volts was established between the burner and a flat, 
circular mesh electrode suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner. The motion of the 
charged ions, which are naturally

passages.text:
olts was established between the burner and a flat, 
circular mesh electrode suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner. The motion of the 
charged ions, which are naturally produced within the flame, are strongly affected by a strong 
electric field. The resulting ion-driven wind can dramatically influence the stability and sooting 
behavior of the flame. Measurements were made of electric-field strength, the ion current 
passing through the flame, and flame characteristics such as the size, structure, temperature, 
soot, and stability. Conducting the tests in microgravity allowed for great simplifications in the 
analysis of ion-driven convection and flame interaction, enabling new understanding and the 
development of less polluting and more efficient combustion technology for use on Earth.

An electric field can strongly influence flames because of its effect on the ions produced as a 
result of the combustion reactions. The induced ion wind can modify the flame shape, alter the 
soot and stability limits, and direct the heat transfer. The purpose of the E-FIELD Flames 
experiment is to gain an improved understanding of flame ion production and learn how the 
electric field can be used to manipulate the ions and control non-premixed flames for practical 
benefit. For example, electric fields can enable stable burner operation at fuel-lean conditions 
with reduced pollutant emission, i.e., where the flame is not reliably sustained without the 
electric field. As another example, the role of electric fields on soot formation can be dramatic. 
It appears that the ion driven wind alters the local convection and strongly influences the 
residence time of the soot precursors within the hot flame. The experiment contributes to our 
critical understanding of combustion processes i

residence time of the soot precursors within the hot flame. The experiment contributes to our 
critical understanding of combustion processes in the presence of electric fields. 
 
More specifically, E-FIELD Flames has the following experimental objectives: 
A. Determine the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as 
functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and the amount of inert 
(nitrogen) in the fuel. 
B. Obtain the time response of the flame chemiluminescence, luminosity, and the ion 
current to large step changes in voltage, as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) 
flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream. 
C. Evaluate and manipulate sooting behavior (i.e., soot volume fraction and location of 
luminous soot) in relation to the electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions 
of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to 
the fuel stream. 
D. Use the variation of the chemi-ion current as a function of applied volta

the fuel stream. 
D. Use the variation of the chemi-ion current as a function of applied voltage to characterize 
the combustion behavior of near-limit lifted flames and use the associated ion-driven 
wind to stabilize or reattach these flames. 
 
The effect of the electric field on the flame is studied through tests conducted with a range of 
flame and electric field conditions. The fuel, fuel jet velocity, air flow, electric-field voltage and 
polarity were the primary parameters of the E-FIELD Flames experiment. Tests were conducted 
with methane and ethylene, including nitrogen dilutions of each, which provide a broad range of 
soot-producing conditions, i.e., from soot-free to highly sooting. They were carried out with both 
a simple gas-jet burner and the coflow burner that was also used for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion 
Flame (CLD Flame) experiment. Tests with the coflow burner were conducted with and without 
a coflow of air, where the results of the latter are compared with those from the g

Flame (CLD Flame) experiment. Tests with the coflow burner were conducted with and without 
a coflow of air, where the results of the latter are compared with those from the gas-jet burner 
to assess the effect of air entrainment on the flame. The coflow burner also provided a different 
electrode configuration (close to a plane-to-plane) than the jet burner (close to a point-to-plane). 
In a typical test, the mesh electrode was energized at increasing potentials (relative to the 
burner), where the flame’s response (e.g., ion current, luminosity, shape) to the resulting field 
strength was measured. The field strength was changed in repeated steps or was instead 
smoothly ramped. 
 
Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages 
over normal-gravity studies. For example, the natural flicker of flames, which is a buoyancy-

driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. 
Therefore, the flicker in the E-FIELD Flames was a result of electric body forces alone. Length 
scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. 
Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be 
studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger 
sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-
gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in 
microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot 
free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and 
stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. For example, chemi-ion species, 
electronically excited chemiluminescent species, ar

stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. For example, chemi-ion species, 
electronically excited chemiluminescent species, are at very low concentration in typical flames, 
making the reduced buoyancy environment valuable for evaluating the minor species chemistry. 
With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex 
nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion 
application. 
 
 
II. Methods/Research Operations 
 
A. Discussion of Method/Protocol 
E-FIELD Flames and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the 
ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. 
The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack 
(CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. 
 
All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload 
Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a 
nom

passages.text:
All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload 
Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a 
nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. However, it may alternately 
be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in 
response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry 
stream. For example, the mesh voltage can be adjusted to approach a flame’s stability or 
soot limit. This was not done during Increments 55-56 or 57-58, where the console 
commanding during a test was typically limited to halting the test when it was observed 
in the analog ops video that the flame had extinguished. 
 
Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to 
ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. 
 
Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary 
analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.

III. Results 
A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight 
A total of 219 flames were ignited for the E-FIELD Flames experiment, with 142 and 77 
respectively ignited during Increments 55-56 and 57-58. Note that the investigation’s 
testing was completed during Increment 57, so no flames were ignited during Increment 
58. The first and second rounds of testing respectively occurred in March-May 2018 and 
September-November 2018. The two rounds of tests resulted in 120 and 99 ignited 
flames conducted with coflow and gas-jet burners, respectively. The coflow burner was 
developed for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment, where CLD 
Flames’ second round occurred between the two rounds of the E-FIELD Flames 
experiment. The ‘interruption’ in the E-FIELD Flames testing was intentionally planned 
years in advance to enable the PI team to review the initial results in detail and with that 
knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize its

years in advance to enable the PI team to review the initial results in detail and with that 
knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize its scientific outcome. 
 
E-FIELD Flames does not have living subjects like a life science experiment, but the tests 
are independently conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene. 
Both are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood. Methane 
(CH4) is the primary component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot 
given the absence of carbon-carbon bonds. Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is highly sooting 
because of its carbon double bond. For both fuels, tests were conducted with pure fuel 
and fuel mixed with nitrogen over a broad range of dilutions. For limited cases, the fuel 
and nitrogen was premixed on the ground prior to launch. ACME bottles were launched 
with methane concentrations of 30%, 40%, 45%, and 100% with a balance of nitrogen (on 
a volume basis). Similarly, bottles were launched with ethylene concentrations of 30%, 
50%, and 100%, ag

a volume basis). Similarly, bottles were launched with ethylene concentrations of 30%, 
50%, and 100%, again with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis). But the ACME 
hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and nitrogen to the burner, allowing 
for on-orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of fuel concentrations. In all cases, 
the coflow was 21% oxygen with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis). 
 
No samples (e.g., of soot) were collected for E-FIELD Flames; all of the ISS results were 
electronically transmitted to the ground. That is furthermore the case for all currently 
planned ACME experiments.

E-FIELD Flames tests sometimes automatically aborted (due to the controlling

igniter. As a result, there was little lost other than the time in the failed test attempt. 
The aborts normally occurred because of communication issues with IPSU-1. These 
are infrequent, but there are some days when te

are infrequent, but there are some days when tests aborted repeatedly. 
 
Tests are of course also unsuccessful when the flame fails to ignite. The first test of 
the day has sometimes failed to ignite, presumably because the fuel line has not been 
sufficiently primed. Ignition was sometimes unsuccessful because the settings for the 
automatic flame detection are such that detection threshold is reached because of 
the igniter glow rather than a flame. As a result of the detection, the hot-wire igniter 
is deactivated and retracted, which is of course an issue if the flame has yet to ignite. 
This is typically avoided by detecting ignition with measurement of the flame’s OH* 
chemiluminescence with a Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) module. The OH* 
chemiluminescence, in the ultraviolet at 310 nm, is a good indicator of an ignited 
flame rather than the glowing igniter, which emits primarily in the infrared and visible 
spectrum. However, the combination of

flame rather than the glowing igniter, which emits primarily in the infrared and visible 
spectrum. However, the combination of igniter settings and PMT gains can lead to 
false ignition detection. 
 
ACME’s Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) used to control the flow of fuel, nitrogen, and 
synthetic air (i.e., 21% oxygen with a balance of nitrogen, on a volume basis) have 
unfortunately not always performed adequately. The fuel and especially nitrogen 
flows sometimes oscillate. Furthermore, the MFC used for the ‘air’ coflow behaves as 
if it is sticking in a few places, where the flow rate won’t linearly ramp when 
commanded (as required for the CLD Flame experiment). It tends to stick in some 
places and then abruptly overshoot where that has sometimes been seen to 
extinguish the flame. As a result, mass flow controllers are tested - without flames - 
after they are first installed. Adjustments are often then made to (1) the settings that 
control when the valves open and (2) the Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) 
settings. This

control when the valves open and (2) the Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID)

18046, 18143, 18241, 19059, and 19112. In this regard, there are an assortment of

FIELD Flames’ first round. Later, a procedure of re-zeroing the MFCs prior to each test 
was also implemented during E-FIELD Flames’ second round. A replacement MFC for 
the ‘air’ coflow is being prepared for spaceflight, where a limited third round of CLD 
Flame testing is being planned to accomplish its extinction limit objective. 
 
C. Completeness/Quality of Data 
The number of flames ignited significantly exceeds the planned tests which were (1) 
specified as required in the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD), 
using the gas-jet burner, and (2) later expanded to include tests with the coflow burner 
to partially make up for science loss resulting from the slow response time of the high-
voltage power supply. Following the revision, a total of 74 E-FIELD Flames tests were 
identified as required. In contras

identified as required. In contrast, 219 flames were ignited in the experiment, so nearly 
three times as many flames were ignited than required. 
 
It should be understood that a complete set of image data is not available for all tests. As 
discussed in section III.B, the IPSU-1 was not working at the beginning of the second round 
of testing, preventing use of both the HiBMs camera and the CIR’s collimated illumination 
package. Those are not critical for E-FIELD Flames, so tests continued without their use. 
 
Furthermore, recorded image data is sometimes deleted without downlinking. This is 
done because of operational constraints which limit the amount of data that can be 
managed per test day. Given the constraint, the decision is sometimes made to sacrifice 
some image data (e.g., from the HiBMs camera) to allow additional tests to be conducted.

Data quality is of course dependent on the experimental hardware. But neglecting that 
limitation on data quality, the cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels gradually 
become ‘hot’ over time. While these bright spots are addressed in image post-processing, 
they are a degradation of the image quality. 
 
It is possible that the tests are subtly affected by the acceleration environment, but there 
is not obvious indication of this and it has thus far not been evaluated with available 
measurements from the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS). In this regard, 
note that the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), in which the experiment is conducted, is 
equipped with a Passive Rack Isolation System (PaRIS).

D. Status of Data Analysis 
Data from the tests making up the E-FIELD Flames experiment includes video recordings 
from the operations camera for general flame behavior, high resolution images from the 
ACME data camera at various exposures and frame rates as dictated by the flame 
luminosity, intensified camera images, and non-imaging data at 125 Hz. The non-imaging 
data file is processed using Matlab scripts (modified from those developed by CLD Flame 
researchers) to separately show trends of ion current and flame luminosity as a function 
of the applied field, and the flame parameters (fuel, flowrate, burner type). The PMT data 
is also extracted to evaluate flame luminosity oscillations. Image data is processed using 
the OMA software (also developed and used by CLD Flame researchers). 
 
The overall data volume is large with a storage limit of 127,000 MB per test day. All of 
the data has been downloaded to the hard drive with a backup system at UC Irvine. At 
this stage, the dat

a volume is large with a storage limit of 127,000 MB per test day. All of 
the data has been downloaded to the hard drive with a backup system at UC Irvine. At 
this stage, the data has been sorted into appropriate segments so that comparisons can 
be made between burner geometries (jet versus coflow from the prior round of testing), 
fuel type and dilution (methane versus ethylene; no dilution, modest dilution, high 
dilution) and fuel flow velocity. The fuel flow velocity and dilution conditions were 
sometimes selected to hold total carbon flux into the flame constant. At this stage, the 
analysis remains comparative and qualitative, to show the major differences in behavior 
in microgravity and normal-gravity (1-g) flames, and to show particularly how buoyancy 
modifies the electrical response of the flames. 
 
E. Preliminary Research Findings 
Distinctly different results were seen in E-FIELD Flames’ second round tests with the gas-
jet burner when compared with the first round tests with the coflow burner. For example, 
the ion current response to the electric field strength wi

econd round tests with the gas-
jet burner when compared with the first round tests with the coflow burner. For example, 
the ion current response to the electric field strength with an upward ion driven wind in 
microgravity is a clear parabolic trend (which is similar to the trend observed in 1-g flames 
with the coflow burner as presented in the prior report). The parabolic behavior is evident 
even with the strong oscillations observed during the rise. This rising trend is not 
observed with the coflow burner. 
 
The behavior of the soot and its charge state are complicated since in the regions of high 
field strength, particularly near the fuel tube where the field lines converge, soot can emit 
or collect free charges. Hence, the soot transport is driven directly by the field and by the 
ion-driven wind (and thermophoresis) which means it can travel differentially to the bulk 
flow. These various transport elements can push the soot through the flame to burnout, 
hold it in stasis in the flame for additional growth, or drive it to the burner where it 
accumulates. More work is

hold it in stasis in the flame for additional growth, or drive it to the burner where it 
accumulates. More work is needed to sort through these elements.

soot region diminishes as the flame shrinks.

Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) 
 
PURPOSE: ACME is focused on advanced combustion 
technology via fundamental microgravity research. The
